1.pericope_label: God, who at sundry times and in divers manners spake in time past unto the fathers by the prophets,

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin take the author of the revelation and the meaning of the two adverbs. Gill says the apostle begins the epistle with an account of the revelation God has made of his mind and will in former times: the author of this revelation is God, not essentially but personally considered, even God the Father, as distinguished from his Son in the next verse, for the revelation under the Old Testament is divine as well as that under the New, and in this they both agree, in whatsoever else they differ. This revelation was made at several times, at different seasons and to different persons, Gill says, and consisted of a variety of things relating to doctrine and worship and concerning the Messiah, of whom at different times there were gradual discoveries made, both before and after the giving of the law, from the beginning of the world and in the times of the patriarchs, of Moses, David, Isaiah and other prophets; and this was delivered in various manners, sometimes by angels, sometimes in a dream, at other times by a vision, and sometimes by Urim and Thummim. Calvin says this beginning is for the purpose of commending the doctrine taught by Christ, for it shows that we ought not only reverently to receive it but also to be satisfied with it alone; and that we may understand this more clearly we must observe the contrast between each of the clauses: first the Son of God is set in opposition to the prophets, then we to the fathers, and thirdly the various and manifold modes of speaking which God had adopted as to the fathers, to the last revelation brought to us by Christ. But in this diversity he still sets before us but one God, Calvin says, that no one might think that the Law militates against the Gospel, or that the author of one is not the author of the other; the agreement between the Law and the Gospel is established, for God, who is ever like himself and whose word is the same and whose truth is unchangeable, has spoken as to both in common. But we must notice the difference between us and the fathers, Calvin says, for God formerly addressed them in a way different from that which he adopts towards us now: as to them he employed the prophets, but he has appointed his Son to be an ambassador to us, so that our condition in this respect is superior to that of the fathers; even Moses is to be classed among the prophets, as he is one of the number of those who are inferior to the Son. In the manner also in which revelation was made we have an advantage over them, Calvin says, for the diversity as to visions and other means adopted under the Old Testament was an indication that it was not yet a fixed state of things, as when matters are put completely in order: God would have followed the same mode perpetually to the end had the mode been perfect and complete, and it hence follows that this variety was an evidence of imperfection. The two words Calvin understands thus: one refers to a diversity as to times, the other points out a diversity in the very manner itself. Some of the fathers, such as Chrysostom, regarded the two words as meaning the same thing, Calvin says, but there is no reason for this; on the contrary, each word has a distinct meaning, one expressing a variety as to parts or portions and the other a variety as to the mode or manner. The parts refer to the different portions of revelation communicated to holy men in different ages of the world, and the second word designates the various modes of communication, by visions, dreams, interposition of angels, and speaking face to face as the case was with Moses; and there was another variety in the manner, sometimes in plain language and at another time in similitudes and parables. When he speaks of the last days, Calvin adds, he intimates that there is no longer any reason to expect any new revelation, for it was not a word in part that Christ brought, but the final conclusion.

Henry takes the two dispensations and the gradual opening of the promise. Here the apostle begins with a general declaration of the excellency of the gospel dispensation above that of the law, Henry says, which he demonstrates from the different way and manner of God's communicating himself and his mind and will to men in the one and in the other: both these dispensations were of God and both very good, but there is a great difference in the way of their coming from God. The persons by whom God delivered his mind under the Old Testament were the prophets, that is, persons chosen of God and qualified by him for that office of revealing the will of God to men, Henry says: no man takes this honour to himself unless called, and whoever are called of God are qualified by him. The persons to whom God spoke by the prophets were the fathers, all the Old Testament saints who were under that dispensation, whom God favoured and honoured with much clearer light than that of nature, under which the rest of the world were left. At sundry times, or by several parts as the word signifies, may refer either to the several ages of the Old Testament dispensation, the patriarchal, the Mosaic and the prophetic, Henry says, or to the several gradual openings of his mind concerning the Redeemer: to Adam, that the Messiah should come of the seed of the woman; to Abraham, that he should spring from his loins; to Jacob, that he should be of the tribe of Judah; to David, that he should be of his house; to Micah, that he should be born at Bethlehem; to Isaiah, that he should be born of a virgin. In divers manners, according to the different ways in which God thought fit to communicate his mind to his prophets, Henry says: sometimes by the illapses of his Spirit, sometimes by dreams, sometimes by visions, sometimes by an audible voice, sometimes by legible characters under his own hand, as when he wrote the ten commandments on tables of stone; and of some of these different ways God himself gave an account in the book of Numbers, that if there be a prophet among you, the Lord will make himself known to him in a vision and will speak to him in a dream, but not so with his servant Moses, with whom he will speak mouth to mouth, even apparently and not in dark speeches. The times of the gospel are the last times, Henry says, and the gospel revelation is the last we are to expect from God: there was first the natural revelation, then the patriarchal by dreams, visions and voices, then the Mosaic in the law given forth and written down, then the prophetic in explaining the law and giving clearer discoveries of Christ; but now we must expect no new revelation, but only more of the Spirit of Christ to help us better to understand what is already revealed. The excellency of the gospel revelation above the former consists in this, that it is the final, the finishing revelation, given forth in the last days of divine revelation, to which nothing is to be added, but the canon of scripture is to be settled and sealed, so that now the minds of men are no longer kept in suspense by the expectation of new discoveries, but they rejoice in a complete revelation of the will of God.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson take the design of the Epistle, the arrangement of the words and the structure of the sentence. Barnes says the main object of the epistle is to commend the Christian religion to those addressed in it in such a way as to prevent defection from it, and that this is done principally by showing its superiority to the Mosaic system. The great danger of Christians in Palestine was of relapsing into the Jewish system, Barnes says: the imposing nature of its rites, the public sentiment in its favour, the fact of its antiquity and its undisputed divine origin would all tend to that, and to counteract this the writer shows that the gospel had higher claims on their attention and that if that were rejected ruin was inevitable. In doing this he begins in this chapter by showing the superiority of the Author of Christianity to prophets and to the angels, that is, that he had a rank entitling him to the profoundest regard; and the drift of the chapter is to show the dignity and exalted nature of the Author of the Christian system. Barnes sets out the chapter under four heads: the announcement that God, who had formerly spoken by the prophets, had in this last dispensation spoken by his Son; the statement of his rank and dignity, as Heir of all things, Creator of the worlds, brightness of the divine glory and upholder of all things; the work and exaltation of the Author of the Christian system, who by his own unassisted agency purified us from our sins and is seated at the right hand of God; and the proofs that what is ascribed to him belongs to him, particularly that he is superior to the angels. The commencement of this epistle varies from all the others which Paul wrote, Barnes notes: in every other instance he at first announces his name and the name of the church or of the individual to whom he wrote. Ellicott says the fine arrangement of the words in the Authorised version fails, it must be confessed, to convey the emphasis which is designed in the original: the writer's object is to place the former revelation over against that which has now been given, and the remarkable words with which the chapter opens, which might not inaptly serve as the motto of the whole Epistle, strike the first note of contrast. If we may imitate the artistic arrangement of the Greek, Ellicott says, the verse will run thus: in many portions and in many ways God having of old spoken unto the fathers in the prophets. To the fathers of the Jewish people God's word was given part by part and in divers manners: it came in the revelations of the patriarchal age, in the successive portions of Holy Writ, various truths being successively unveiled through the varying ministry of law and of prophecy and of promise, ever growing clearer through the teaching of experience and history; at one time the word came in direct precept, at another in typical ordinance or act, at another in parable or psalm. The word thus dealt out in fragments and variously imparted was God's word, Ellicott says, for the revealing Spirit of God was in the prophets; and we must not unduly limit the application of prophet, since besides those to whom the name is directly given there were many who were representatives of God to his people and interpreters of his will. Robertson says this Epistle begins like Genesis and the Fourth Gospel with God, who is the Author of the old revelation in the prophets and of the new in his Son, and that the first three verses are a proem or introduction to the whole Epistle. The periodic structure of the sentence reminds one of the prefaces to Luke, Romans and the First Epistle of John, Robertson says: the sentence could have concluded with the words in a Son, but by means of three relatives the author presents the Son as the exact counterpart of God. Of old time means long ago; having spoken is the first aorist active participle of a verb originally used of the chattering of birds and then of the highest form of speech, as here; unto the fathers means the Old Testament worthies in general, without our or your; in the prophets means as the quickening power of their life. By divers portions is an adverb from a late adjective found in the papyri, here only in the New Testament, and the Old Testament revelation came at different times and in various stages, a progressive revelation of God to men; in divers manners is an adverb from an old adjective, only here in the New Testament. The two adverbs together are a sonorous hendiadys for variously, Robertson says, as Chrysostom took them: God spoke by dream, by direct voice, by signs, in different ways to different men.

Clarke and Wesley take the character of the Epistle and the finality of the revelation. The Epistle to the Hebrews is by far the most important and useful of all the apostolic writings, Clarke says: all the doctrines of the Gospel are in it embodied, illustrated and enforced in a manner the most lucid, by references and examples the most striking, and by arguments the most cogent and convincing. It is an epitome of the dispensations of God to man from the foundation of the world to the advent of Christ, Clarke says, not only the sum of the Gospel but the sum and completion of the Law, on which it is also a most beautiful and luminous comment: without this the law of Moses had never been fully understood, nor God's design in giving it. The apostle appears to have taken a portion of one of his own epistles for his text, that Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to them that believe, and has most amply demonstrated his proposition, Clarke says; all the rites, ceremonies and sacrifices of the Mosaic institution are shown to have had Christ for their object and end. Never were premises more clearly stated, never was an argument handled in a more masterly manner, and never was a conclusion more legitimately and satisfactorily brought forth, Clarke says: the matter is everywhere the most interesting, the manner throughout the most engaging, and the language most beautifully adapted to the whole, pure and elegant as that of the most accomplished Grecian orators, and harmonious and diversified as the music of the spheres; the work may be read a hundred times over without perceiving any thing of sameness, and with new and increased information at each reading. To explain and illustrate this epistle multitudes have toiled hard, Clarke adds, and I also will show my opinion, and ten thousand may succeed me and still bring out something that is new. That it was written to Jews, naturally such, the whole structure of the epistle proves, Clarke says: had it been written to the Gentiles, not one in ten thousand of them could have comprehended the argument, because unacquainted with the Jewish system, the knowledge of which the writer everywhere supposes. He cites a scholar who traced its peculiar diction to Jewish sources and stated the proposition of the whole epistle as this, that Jesus of Nazareth is the true God, in proof of which the apostle uses but three arguments: that Christ is superior to the angels, that he is superior to Moses, and that he is superior to Aaron. These arguments would appear more distinctly were it not for the improper division of the chapters, Clarke complains, since he who divided them in the middle ages, a division to which we are still unreasonably attached, had but a superficial knowledge of the word of God. Wesley says the creation was revealed in the time of Adam and the last judgment in the time of Enoch, and so at various times and in various degrees more explicit knowledge was given; in divers manners means in visions, in dreams, and by revelations of various kinds, both these being opposed to the one entire and perfect revelation which he has made to us by Jesus Christ, and the very number of the prophets showed that they prophesied only in part. Of old, Wesley says, means that there were no prophets for a large tract of time before Christ came, that the great Prophet might be the more earnestly expected; spake is a part put for the whole, implying every kind of divine communication; and the mention of the prophets is a virtual declaration that the apostle received the whole Old Testament and was not about to advance any doctrine in contradiction to it. Hath in these last times intimates that no other revelation is to be expected, Wesley says, and spoken by his Son means all things, and in the most perfect manner, by his Son alone.

Chrysostom takes the pastoral purpose of the opening and the sense of the two adverbs. Truly, where sin abounded grace did much more abound, Chrysostom begins, and this at least the blessed Paul intimates here also, in the very beginning of his Epistle to the Hebrews. For since as it was likely that, afflicted and worn out by evils and judging of things thereby, they would think themselves worse off than all other men, he shows that herein they had rather been made partakers of greater, even very exceeding, grace, arousing the hearer at the very opening of his discourse. Why did Paul not oppose himself to the prophets, Chrysostom asks, since certainly he was much greater than they, inasmuch as a greater trust was committed to him? Yet he doth not so. First, to avoid speaking great things concerning himself; secondly, because his hearers were not yet perfect; and thirdly, because he rather wished to exalt them, and to show that their superiority was great, as if he had said, What so great matter is it that He sent prophets to our fathers? For to us he has sent his own only-begotten Son himself. And well did he begin thus, at sundry times and in divers manners, Chrysostom says, for he points out that not even the prophets themselves saw God; nevertheless, the Son saw Him. For the expressions at sundry times and in divers manners are the same as in different ways: for I, saith He, have multiplied visions, and used similitudes by the ministry of the Prophets. Wherefore the excellency consists not in this alone, that to them indeed prophets were sent, but to us the Son.

debates: Whether the two adverbs mean one thing or two. Chrysostom says the expressions at sundry times and in divers manners are the same as in different ways; Robertson agrees, calling the pair a sonorous hendiadys for variously and citing Chrysostom for it; Calvin names Chrysostom and rejects the reading, holding that one word expresses a variety as to parts or portions and the other a variety as to mode or manner, and builds on the distinction; Henry keeps both senses apart in the same way without raising the question.

What the diversity of the old revelation proves. Calvin makes it evidence of imperfection, since God would have followed one mode perpetually had that mode been perfect and complete; Ellicott makes it a designed progression, truths successively unveiled and ever growing clearer through the teaching of experience and history; Henry lists the ages and the gradual openings without evaluating them; Robertson calls it a progressive revelation of God to men.

Whether any further revelation is to be looked for. Wesley says the phrase intimates that no other is to be expected; Henry says we must expect no new revelation but only more of the Spirit of Christ to help us understand what is revealed, the canon being settled and sealed; Calvin says it was not a word in part that Christ brought but the final conclusion; the three agree without appearing to draw on one another.

What kind of book this is. Barnes describes it as a defensive work written to prevent relapse into a Judaism whose rites, antiquity and public favour made it attractive; Clarke describes it as the most important and useful of all the apostolic writings and an epitome of the dispensations of God to man; Robertson describes it formally, as an Epistle that begins like Genesis with God and whose first sentence is a periodic proem.
outliers: Chrysostom alone reads the opening as consolation rather than argument, taking the hearers to be afflicted men who thought themselves worse off than others, and the first sentence as a way of arousing them by showing that they had been given more, not less.

Chrysostom alone asks why Paul did not set himself against the prophets, since a greater trust had been committed to him, and answers that he avoided speaking great things of himself, that his hearers were not yet perfect, and that he wished to exalt them instead.

Clarke alone breaks into praise of the Epistle as literature, calling its language pure and elegant as that of the most accomplished Grecian orators and as harmonious and diversified as the music of the spheres, and saying it may be read a hundred times over without any sense of sameness.

Clarke alone attacks the chapter divisions, saying that the man who made them in the middle ages had but a superficial knowledge of the word of God and that the argument of the Epistle would appear more distinctly without them.

2.pericope_label: Hath in these last days spoken unto us by his Son, whom he hath appointed heir of all things, by whom also he made the worlds;

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin take the last days and the heirship. Gill says this is the Gospel revelation, or the revelation in the Gospel dispensation, which though it comes from the same author the other does, yet in many things differs from it and is preferable to it, the general design of this epistle being to show the superior excellency of the one to the other. The former was delivered out in time past, but this in these last days, Gill says; the Alexandrian copy, the Complutensian edition and several other copies read, in the last of these days, perfectly agreeable to the Hebrew phrase to which the apostle refers, and in which places the days of the Messiah are intended; and it is a rule with the Jews that wherever the phrase the last days is mentioned, the days of the Messiah are designed. They are to be understood not of the last days of the natural world, Gill says, but of the Jewish world and state, though indeed the times of the Messiah may be called the last days of the natural world according to the tradition of the house of Elias. Calvin says he honours Christ with high commendations in order to lead us to show him reverence, for since the Father has subjected all things to him we are all under his authority; he also intimates that no good can be found apart from him, as he is the heir of all things, whence it follows that we must be very miserable and destitute of all good things except he supplies us with his treasures. He further adds that this honour of possessing all things belongs by right to the Son, Calvin says, because by him have all things been created; at the same time, heirship and creation are ascribed to Christ for different reasons. The world was created by him as he is the eternal wisdom of God, which is said to have been the director of all his works from the beginning, and hence is proved the eternity of Christ, for he must have existed before the world was created by him; if the duration of his time be inquired of, it will be found that it has no beginning. Nor is it any derogation to his power that he is said to have created the world, as though he did not by himself create it, Calvin says: according to the most usual mode of speaking in Scripture the Father is called the Creator, and it is added in some places that the world was created by wisdom, by the word, by the Son, as though wisdom itself had been the creator. But we must observe that there is a difference of persons between the Father and the Son, not only with regard to men but with regard to God himself, Calvin says, while the unity of essence requires that whatever is peculiar to Deity should belong to the Son as well as to the Father, and yet there is nothing in this to prevent each from having his own peculiar properties. The word heir is ascribed to Christ as manifested in the flesh, Calvin says, for being made man he put on our nature and as such received this heirship, and that for this purpose, that he might restore to us what we had lost in Adam. For God had at the beginning constituted man, as his Son, the heir of all good things, but through sin the first man became alienated from God and deprived himself and his posterity of all good things, as well as of the favour of God; we hence only then begin to enjoy by right the good things of God when Christ, the universal heir, admits us to a union with himself, for he is an heir that he may endow us with his riches. The Apostle adorns him with this title that we may know that without him we are destitute of all good things, Calvin says, and we are driven from the legitimate possession of all things, both in heaven and on earth, except we be united to Christ.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson take the last dispensation, the anarthrous Son and the heirship. Barnes says in these last days means in this final dispensation, or the dispensation under which the affairs of the world will be wound up: phrases similar to this occur frequently in the Scriptures, and they do not imply that the world was soon coming to an end, but that this was the last dispensation, the last period of the world. There had been the patriarchal period, the period under the law, the prophets and the rest, Barnes says, and this was the period during which God's last method of communication would be enjoyed and under which the world would close: it might be a very long period, but it would be the last one, and it might be the longest period, or longer than all the others put together, but still it would be the last one. The word us does not of necessity imply that the writer of the epistle had actually heard him, or that they had heard him to whom the epistle was written, Barnes says; it means that God had now communicated his will to man by his Son, and it may be said with entire propriety that God has spoken to us by his Son though we have not personally heard or seen him, since we have what he spoke, and caused to be recorded, for our direction. By his Son is the title commonly given to the Lord Jesus as denoting his peculiar relation to God, Barnes says, and it was understood by the Jews to denote equality with God and is used with such a reference here; it is implied that the fact that the Son of God has spoken to us imposes the highest obligations to attend to what he has said, that he has authority superior to all those who have spoken in past times, and that there will be peculiar guilt in refusing to attend to what he has spoken. The reasons for the superior respect which should be shown to his revelations are his rank and dignity, since he is equal with God and is himself called God in this chapter, and the clearness of the truths which he communicated on a great variety of subjects of the highest moment. Revelation has been gradual, Barnes says, like the breaking of the day in the east: at first there is a little light, it increases and expands till objects become more and more visible, and then the sun rises in full-orbed glory; at first we discern only the existence of some object, obscure and undefined, then we can trace its outline, then its colour, its size, its proportions, its drapery, till it stands before us fully revealed. Among the subjects we now see clearly which were very imperfectly understood by the teaching of the prophets, Barnes says, are the character of God, whom Christ came to make known as a merciful Being and to show how he could be merciful as well as just, and the way in which man may be reconciled to God. Ellicott renders it, at the end of these days spake unto us in a Son: the thought common to the two verses is that God hath spoken to man, and in all other respects the past and the present stand contrasted, the manifold successive partial disclosures of God's will having given place to one revelation, complete and final. The whole stress lies on the last words, Ellicott says: the rendering a Son may at first cause surprise, but it is absolutely needed, for the question answered is not who the Revealer is, but what he is. The writer does not speak of a Son in the sense of one out of many, Ellicott says: the very contrast with the prophets, who in the lower sense were amongst God's sons, would be sufficient to prove this, but the words which follow and the whole contents of this chapter are designed to show the supreme dignity of him who is God's latest Representative on earth; the prophet's commission extended no farther than the special message of his words and life, while a Son spoke with his Father's authority and with complete knowledge of his will and purpose. It is impossible to read these first lines, in which the whole argument of the Epistle is enfolded, without recalling the prologue of the fourth Gospel, Ellicott says: the name Word is not mentioned here and the highest level of that teaching is not reached, but the idea which the Word expresses, and the thought of the Only Begotten as declaring and interpreting the Father, are present throughout. There is something unusual in the words at the end of these days, Ellicott adds: Peter speaks of the manifestation of Christ at the end of the times, and both in the Old Testament and in the New we not unfrequently read at the end, or in the last, of the days; the peculiarity here lies in these days, for the ages preceding and following the appearance of Messiah are in Jewish writers known as this world and the coming world, and the end of these days would be understood by every Jewish reader to denote the time of his appearing. Whom he hath appointed is better, whom he appointed: in the divine counsels he was constituted Heir of all things, Ellicott says, and the clauses which follow describe the successive steps in the accomplishment of this purpose. The words have often been understood as referring to the Son's essential Lordship, as Eternal Son he is and must be Heir of all, Ellicott says, but this explanation is less consistent with the word appointed, with the strict significance of Heir, and with the development of the thought in the following verses, and it is on all grounds more probable that in these words is expressed the great theme of the Epistle, the consummation of all things in the Christ. By whom is rather through whom, as in the fourth Gospel all things came into being through the Word and in Colossians all things have been created through him; a scholar is quoted that this mediatorial function has entirely changed its character, since to the Alexandrian Jew it was the work of a passive tool or instrument, but to the Christian Apostle it represented a co-operating agent. Robertson notes that at the end of these days stands in contrast with the of old above, and that hath spoken is a first aorist, did speak in a final and full revelation. In his Son is in sharp contrast with in the prophets, Robertson says: there is no article or pronoun here with the preposition, giving the absolute sense of Son, and the idea is not merely what Jesus said but what he is, God's Son who reveals the Father; the Old Testament, he quotes, slopes upward to Christ, and the revelation was a Son. Hath appointed is a timeless aorist, and the idea of sonship easily passes into that of heirship; the Son as Heir is also the Intermediate Agent in the work of creation. The worlds is literally the ages, Robertson says, and the original sense of the word occurs elsewhere in this Epistle, but here it stands by metonymy of the container for the contained for the worlds, the universe.

Clarke and Wesley take the missing pronoun and the order of the titles. Last days means the Gospel dispensation, called the last days and the last time because not to be followed by any other dispensation, Clarke says, or the conclusion of the Jewish Church and state now at their termination. It is very remarkable that the pronoun his is not found in the text, Clarke says, nor is it found in any manuscript or version; we should not therefore supply the pronoun as our translators have done, but simply read, by a Son, or in a Son, whom he hath appointed heir of all things. God has many sons and daughters, for he is the Father of the spirits of all flesh, Clarke says, and he has many heirs, for if sons, then heirs, heirs of God and joint heirs with Jesus Christ; but he has no Son who is heir of all things, none by whom he made the worlds, none in whom he speaks and by whom he has delivered a complete revelation to mankind, but Jesus the Christ. The apostle begins with the lowest state in which Christ has appeared, Clarke says, his being a Son, born of a woman and made under the law; he then ascends to his being an Heir, and an Heir of all things; then describes him as the Creator of all worlds; as the Brightness of the divine glory; as the express Image of his person; as sustaining the immense fabric of the universe, and this by the word of his power; as having made an atonement for the sin of the world, which was the most stupendous of all his works, since it was great to speak a world from nought but greater to redeem; as being on the right hand of God, infinitely exalted above all created beings and the object of adoration to all the angelic host; as having an eternal throne, neither his person nor his dignity ever changing or decaying; and as continuing to exercise dominion when the earth and the heavens are no more. It is only in God manifested in the flesh that all these excellences can possibly appear, Clarke says, and therefore the apostle begins this astonishing climax with the simple Sonship of Christ, or his incarnation, for on this all that he is to man and all that he has done for man is built. Wesley says that after the name of Son his inheritance is mentioned: God appointed him the heir long before he made the worlds, the Son being the firstborn, born before all things, while heir is a term relating to the creation which followed. By whom he also made the worlds, Wesley says, therefore the Son was before all worlds, and his glory reaches from everlasting to everlasting, though God spake by him to us only in these last days.

Cyril takes the Son as Maker. Christ then is the Only-begotten Son of God, and Maker of the world, Cyril says, for he was in the world, and the world was made by him, and he came unto his own, as the Gospel teaches us. And not only of the things which are seen, but also of the things which are not seen, is Christ the Maker at the Father's bidding, Cyril says: for in him, according to the Apostle, were all things created that are in the heavens and that are upon the earth, things visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or principalities or powers, all things having been created by him and for him, and he is before all, and in him all things consist. Even if thou speak of the worlds, of these also Jesus Christ is the Maker by the Father's bidding, Cyril says, for in these last days God spake unto us by his Son, whom he appointed heir of all things, by whom also he made the worlds; to whom be the glory, honour and might, now and ever, and world without end.

debates: When the heirship began. Wesley puts it before the creation, God having appointed him heir long before he made the worlds, the Son being firstborn and born before all things; Calvin refers the title to Christ as manifested in the flesh, since being made man he received the heirship in order to restore what was lost in Adam; Ellicott rejects the reading that as Eternal Son he must be Heir of all, holding it less consistent with the word appointed and with the strict significance of heir, and takes the words for the great theme of the Epistle, the consummation of all things in the Christ.

What the absence of the article before Son does. Clarke says the pronoun his is in no manuscript or version and should not have been supplied, so that the text reads in a Son; Ellicott says the rendering may cause surprise but is absolutely needed, the question answered being not who the Revealer is but what he is; Robertson says the absence of article and pronoun gives the absolute sense of Son, the point being not what Jesus said but what he is.

What the end of these days means. Gill reports copies reading in the last of these days and cites the Jewish rule that the last days always denote the days of the Messiah, taking them to be the last days of the Jewish state and not of the natural world; Ellicott reaches the same conclusion from the Jewish division of time into this world and the coming world; Barnes uses the phrase to argue only that this is the final dispensation, which might be longer than all the others put together and still be the last; Clarke says simply that no other dispensation is to follow.

What the worlds means. Robertson says the Greek word is the ages, used here by metonymy of the container for the contained for the universe; Calvin argues from the making of the world to the eternity of Christ, who must have existed before it; Cyril extends the word to things not seen, thrones and dominions and principalities and powers; Wesley draws the inference that the Son was before all worlds.
outliers: Clarke alone builds a ten-step climax out of the chapter, ascending from the lowest state in which Christ appeared, a Son born of a woman and made under the law, to his exercising dominion when the earth and the heavens are no more, and remarks that it was great to speak a world from nought but greater to redeem.

Barnes alone defends the word us against a narrow reading, arguing that it may be said with entire propriety that God has spoken to us by his Son though we have neither heard nor seen him, since we have what he spoke and caused to be recorded.

Barnes alone describes the whole history of revelation as a sunrise, a little light at first, increasing till the outline, then the colour, then the proportions of an object can be traced, and then the sun rising in full-orbed glory.
Cyril alone closes his comment with a doxology, quoting the verse itself and adding, to whom be the glory, honour and might, now and ever, and world without end.
themes: hath in these last days spoken unto us
by his Son
heir of all things
by whom also he made the worlds
the absence of the article before Son
the days of the Messiah

3.pericope_label: Who being the brightness of his glory, and the express image of his person, and upholding all things by the word of his power, when he had by himself purged our sins, sat down on the right hand of the Majesty on high;

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin take the figure of the ray and the purpose of the titles. Gill says the brightness is of the glory of God the Father, the God of glory and glory itself, so called on account of his glorious nature and perfections and because of the glorious manifestations of them in his works of creation and providence and in the various dispensations of his grace, and especially in his Son. Christ is the brightness of this, as he is God, Gill says: he has the same glorious nature and perfections, and the same glorious names, as Jehovah, the Lord of glory, and the same glory, homage and worship given him; the allusion is to the sun and its beam or ray, so that some render it the ray of his glory, and this may lead us to observe that the Father and the Son are of the same nature, as the sun and its ray, and that the one is not before the other, and yet they are distinct from each other, and cannot be divided or separated one from another. Calvin says these things are said of Christ partly as to his divine essence and partly as a partaker of our flesh, the whole being stated in order to set forth the dignity of Christ. It is for the same reason that the Son is said to be the brightness of his glory and the impress of his substance, Calvin says: they are words borrowed from nature, for nothing can be said of things so great and so profound but by similitudes taken from created things. There is therefore no need refinedly to discuss the question how the Son, who has the same essence with the Father, is a brightness emanating from his light, Calvin says: we must allow that there is a degree of impropriety in the language when what is borrowed from created things is transferred to the hidden majesty of God, but still the things which are evident to our senses are fitly applied to God, and for this end, that we may know what is to be found in Christ and what benefits he brings to us. It ought also to be observed that frivolous speculations are not here taught but an important doctrine of faith, Calvin says: we ought therefore to apply these high titles given to Christ for our own benefit, for they bear a relation to us. When therefore thou hearest that the Son is the brightness of the Father's glory, think thus with thyself, that the glory of the Father is invisible until it shines forth in Christ, and that he is called the impress of his substance because the majesty of the Father is hidden until it shows itself impressed as it were on his image. They who overlook this connection and carry their philosophy higher weary themselves to no purpose, Calvin says, for they do not understand the design of the Apostle; for it was not his object to show what likeness the Father bears to the Son, but his purpose was really to build up our faith, so that we may learn that God is made known to us in no other way than in Christ. As to the essence of God, so immense is the brightness that it dazzles our eyes except it shines on us in Christ, Calvin says, and it hence follows that we are blind as to the light of God until in Christ it beams on us; it is indeed a profitable philosophy to learn Christ by the real understanding of faith and experience. The same view is to be taken of the impress, for as God is in himself to us incomprehensible, his form appears to us only in his Son.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson take the reference of the description, the words for brightness and image, and the exaltation. Barnes says this verse is designed to state the dignity and exalted rank of the Son of God and is exceedingly important with reference to a correct view of the Redeemer, every word employed being of great importance. In what manner does it refer to the Redeemer, Barnes asks: to his divine nature, to the mode of his existence before he was incarnate, or to him as he appeared on earth? Most of the ancient commentators supposed that it referred to his divine dignity before he became incarnate, and proceed to argue on that supposition on the mode of the divine existence; but the true solution seems to me to be, Barnes says, that it refers to him as incarnate, but still has reference to him as the incarnate Son of God, to him as Mediator but not simply or mainly as a man, rather to him as divine, thus, in his incarnation, being the brightness of the divine glory. That this is the correct view is apparent from the whole scope of the passage, Barnes says, since the drift of the argument is to show his dignity as he has spoken to us and not in the period antecedent to his incarnation, and it is a description of him as he actually is, the incarnate Son of God, the equal of the Father in human flesh. The word glory properly means a seeming or an appearance, then praise, then dignity and splendour, then brightness and dazzling light, Barnes says, and is probably used here to denote splendour and to refer to the divine perfections as resembling a bright light or the sun: here there is a comparison of God with the sun, for he is encompassed with splendour and majesty and is a being of light and of infinite perfection. The word rendered brightness occurs nowhere else in the New Testament and means properly reflected splendour, or the light which emanates from a luminous body: the rays or beams of the sun are its brightness, or that by which the sun is seen and known, and the sun itself we do not see, while the beams which flow from it we do see. If God be represented under the image of a luminous body, as he is in the Scriptures, then Christ is the radiance of that light, Barnes says, and he is that by which we perceive God, or by which God is made known to us in his real perfections, since it is by him only that the true character and glory of God is known to men. Ellicott renders it, who being the effulgence of his glory and the exact image of his substance, and says the first figure is familiar to us in the words of the Nicene Creed, themselves derived from this verse and a commentary upon it: God of God, Light of Light, Very God of Very God. Striking parallels present themselves in Philo, who speaks of the spirit breathed into man at his creation as an effulgence of the Blessed and Thrice-blessed Nature, and in the well-known passage of the Book of Wisdom, that she, Wisdom, is the effulgence of the everlasting light, the unspotted mirror of the power of God, and the image of his goodness. In the Old Testament the token of the divine presence is the cloud of glory, Ellicott says, but here it is the divine nature itself that is denoted by the glory; of the relation between this word and substance it is difficult to speak, as the conceptions necessarily transcend human language, but we may perhaps say, remembering that all such terms are but figurative, that the latter word is internal and the former external, the latter the essence in itself and the former its manifestation. Thus the Son in his relation to God is represented here by light beaming forth from light, and by exact impress, the perfect image produced by stamp or seal, Ellicott says; and these designations, relating to the essential nature of the Son, have no limitation to time, the participle being must be understood of eternal, continuous existence. The word person is an unfortunate mistranslation in this place, Ellicott adds: most of the earlier English versions have substance, person being first introduced in a sixteenth-century revision. The thought of upholding by the word seems suggested by Genesis, the spoken word being the expression of his power, and what is said of being applies to upholding except that the latter implies a previous creative act. The older manuscripts omit by himself and our, Ellicott says, so that the words must be rendered, when he had made purification of sins: at first the change may seem a loss, but it is easily seen that the simpler statement is more majestic and also more suitable in this place, the more complete explanation of the truth belonging to a later stage. The figure of sitting at the right hand, which we meet with more than twenty times in the New Testament, is throughout derived from the first words of the hundred and tenth Psalm, which are descriptive of the exaltation of the Messiah, Ellicott says: the investiture of the Son of Man with unlimited dominion and supreme dignity, the Saviour's rest after the accomplishment of his work on earth, and his waiting for the complete and final subjection of his enemies, are the ideas signified. Robertson says being denotes absolute and timeless existence in contrast with became in the next verse, like the opening of the fourth Gospel. The word for effulgence is a late substantive, here only in the New Testament but found in Wisdom and in Philo, and it can mean either reflected brightness, refulgence, as Calvin and the lexicon hold, or effulgence, a ray from an original light body, as the Greek fathers hold; both senses are true of Christ in his relation to God, Robertson says, but the meaning effulgence suits the context better, though it gives the idea of eternal generation of the Son. The word for image is an old word from a verb meaning to cut or to scratch or to mark, Robertson says: it first was the agent or tool that did the marking, then the mark or impress made, the exact reproduction, and the word occurs in the inscriptions for person as well as for exact reproduction of a person. The word for substance is a philosophical rather than a religious term, etymologically the sediment or foundation under a building, and Athanasius rightly used these opening verses in his controversy with Arius. Upholding is a present participle closely connected with being, Robertson says, and the newer science as expounded in his own day is in harmony with the spiritual and personal conception of creation here presented. Purification of sins is the first mention of the priestly work of Christ, the keynote of this Epistle; sat down is a first aorist, took his seat, a formal and dignified act; and Christ resumed his original dignity and glory, being here pictured as King, and Prophet and Priest also, seated at the right hand of God.

Clarke and Wesley take the two figures and the significance of the sitting. The brightness of his glory is the resplendent outbeaming of the essential glory of God, Clarke says, and a lexicographer interprets the word as the splendour of the sun; the same form of expression is used in the Book of Wisdom, where, speaking of the uncreated wisdom of God, the writer says that she is the splendour of eternal light and the unsullied mirror of the energy of God and the image of his goodness. One Greek word is that which has splendour in itself, Clarke explains, and the other is the splendour emitted from it, but the inherent splendour and the exhibited splendour are radically and essentially the same. The express image of his person is the character or impression of his substance, Clarke says, and it is supposed that these words expound the former, image expounding brightness and person or substance expounding glory: the substance of God is that which is essential to him as God, and the character or image is that by which all the likeness of the original becomes manifest, and is a perfect facsimile of the whole; it is a metaphor taken from sealing, the die or seal leaving the full impression of its every part on the wax to which it is applied. From these words it is evident, Clarke argues, that the apostle states Jesus Christ to be of the same essence with the Father, as the proceeding splendour must be the same with the inherent splendour; that Christ, though proceeding from the Father, is of the same essence, for if one splendour produce another splendour the produced splendour must be of the same essence with that which produces it; that although Christ is thus of the same essence with the Father, yet he is a distinct person from the Father, as the splendour of the sun, though of the same essence, is distinct from the sun itself, though each is essential to the other; and that Christ is eternal with the Father, as the proceeding splendour must necessarily be coexistent with the inherent splendour, so that if the one be uncreated the other is uncreated, and if the one be eternal the other is eternal. Upholding all things by the word of his power is an astonishing description of the infinitely energetic and all pervading power of God, Clarke says: he spake, and all things were created; he speaks, and all things are sustained; and the Jewish writers frequently express the perfection of the divine nature by the phrases, He bears all things both above and below, He carries all his creatures, He bears his world, He bears all worlds by his power. Clarke sees in the verse a reference to the transactions in the wilderness: Moses, while in communion with God on the mount, was so impressed with the divine glories that his face shone so that the Israelites could not behold it, but Jesus is infinitely greater than Moses, for he is the splendour of God's glory; Moses found the government of the Israelites such a burden that he altogether sank under it, asking whether he had conceived all this people, but Christ upholds all things by the word of his power; and the Israelites would have been consumed had not Aaron made an atonement for them, but Jesus makes an atonement not for Israel only but for the whole world. Wesley says the glory which he received in his exaltation at the right hand of the Father no angel was capable of, but the Son alone, who likewise enjoyed it long before. Glory is the nature of God revealed in its brightness, Wesley says; the express image is or stamp, and whatever the Father is is exhibited in the Son, as a seal in the stamp on wax; of his person, or substance, the word denoting the unchangeable perpetuity of divine life and power. When he had by himself purged our sins means without any Mosaic rites or ceremonies, Wesley says, and in order to this it was necessary he should for a time divest himself of his glory. In this chapter Paul describes his glory chiefly as he is the Son of God, and afterwards the glory of the man Christ Jesus, speaking briefly of the former before his humiliation but copiously after his exaltation. The priests stood while they ministered, Wesley says: sitting, therefore, denotes the consummation of his sacrifice, and this word, sat down, contains the scope, the theme, and the sum, of the epistle.

Chrysostom and Cyril take the reverence due to the subject and the session at the right hand. Everywhere indeed a reverential mind is requisite, Chrysostom says, but especially when we say or hear anything of God, since neither can tongue speak nor thought hear anything suitable to our God. And why speak I of tongue or thought? For not even the understanding, which far excels these, will be able to comprehend anything accurately when we desire to utter aught concerning God; for if the peace of God surpasseth all understanding, and the things prepared for them that love him have not entered into the heart of man, much more he himself, the God of peace, the Creator of all things, doth by a wide measure exceed our reasoning. We ought therefore to receive all things with faith and reverence, Chrysostom says, and when our discourse fails through weakness and is not able to set forth accurately the things which are spoken, then especially to glorify God, for that we have such a God, surpassing both our thought and our conception. For many of our conceptions about God we are unable to express, as also many things we express but have not strength to conceive of them: that God is everywhere, we know, but how, we no longer understand; that there is a certain incorporeal power the cause of all our good things, we know, but how it is, or what it is, we know not. Lo, we speak, and do not understand, Chrysostom says: I said that he is everywhere, but I do not understand it; I said that he is without beginning, but I do not understand it; I said that he begat from himself, and again I know not how I shall understand it; and some things there are which we may not even speak. Cyril says he must remind us also of a few other testimonies concerning the Son's sitting at the right hand of the Father: in the Gospel according to Matthew it is written, Henceforth ye shall see the Son of Man sitting on the right hand of power; in accordance with which the Apostle Peter writes, by the Resurrection of Jesus Christ, who is on the right hand of God, having gone into heaven; and the Apostle Paul, writing to the Romans, says, It is Christ that died, yea rather, that is risen again, who is even at the right hand of God; and charging the Ephesians he speaks of the working of his mighty power, which he wrought in Christ when he raised him from the dead and set him at his own right hand; and the Colossians he taught, if ye then be risen with Christ, seek the things above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God; and in the Epistle to the Hebrews he says, when he had made purification of sins.

debates: Whether the description belongs to the eternal Son or to the incarnate Mediator. Ellicott says the designations relate to the essential nature of the Son and have no limitation to time, the participle meaning eternal and continuous existence; Robertson agrees, calling it absolute and timeless existence in contrast with the became of the next verse; Barnes reports that most of the ancient commentators referred it to the divine dignity before the incarnation and dissents, holding that it describes him as incarnate, the equal of the Father in human flesh; Calvin divides it, partly of the divine essence and partly as he is partaker of our flesh.

Whether the word means reflected or emitted brightness. Robertson sets out both senses, names Calvin for reflected and the Greek fathers for emitted, and judges that emitted suits the context better though it carries the idea of eternal generation; Barnes glosses it as reflected splendour, the light which emanates from a luminous body; Clarke insists that the inherent splendour and the exhibited splendour are radically and essentially the same; Gill says only that the allusion is to the sun and its ray.

How far the speculation should be carried. Chrysostom says neither tongue nor thought nor understanding can comprehend anything accurately concerning God, and confesses that he speaks without understanding what he says; Calvin says they who carry their philosophy higher weary themselves to no purpose and mistake the Apostle's design, which was to build up faith and not to show what likeness the Father bears the Son; Clarke, Ellicott and Robertson proceed with the analysis the other two warn against.

What the closing clauses are worth. Ellicott reports that the older manuscripts omit by himself and our, leaving simply that he made purification of sins, and holds the shorter reading more majestic; Wesley keeps the longer and reads by himself as without any Mosaic rites or ceremonies; Robertson notes the first mention of the priestly work of Christ; Wesley reads the sitting against the standing of the priests, and calls the words sat down the scope, the theme and the sum of the epistle.
outliers: Ellicott alone attacks the English word person as an unfortunate mistranslation, noting that most of the earlier versions read substance and that person entered only with a sixteenth-century revision.

Chrysostom alone turns the comment into a confession of ignorance, saying plainly that he has asserted God to be everywhere, to be without beginning, and to have begotten from himself, and that he understands none of the three.

Clarke alone reads the whole verse against Moses, whose shining face the Israelites could not behold, who sank under the burden of governing one nation, and whose people needed Aaron's atonement, where Christ is the splendour itself, upholds all things, and atones for the world.
Robertson alone reaches for contemporary physics, remarking that the newer science of his own day is in harmony with the spiritual and personal conception of creation set out here.
themes: the brightness of his glory
the express image of his person
upholding all things by the word of his power
purged our sins
sat down on the right hand of the Majesty
the limits of speculation about God

4.pericope_label: Being made so much better than the angels, as he hath by inheritance obtained a more excellent name than they.

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin take the sense of being made and the meaning of the name. Christ is so much better than the angels, Gill says, as the Creator than the creature, as an independent being than a dependent one, as he that blesses than he that is blessed, as he that is worshipped than he that worships, as a king than his subjects, as a master than his servants, and as he that sends than he that is sent. Christ may be said to be made so when he was manifested and declared to be so, Gill says, and he was actually preferred to them and exalted above them in human nature after he had expiated the sins of his people and when he was set down at the right hand of God, with which these words stand connected; for in his state of humiliation, and through his sufferings and death, he was made lower than they, but when he was risen from the dead and ascended to heaven he was placed at the right hand of God, where none of them ever was or ever will be. Besides, Gill adds, the phrase being made signifies no more than that he was. Calvin says that after having raised Christ above Moses and all others, he now amplifies his glory by a comparison with angels. It was a common notion among the Jews that the Law was given by angels, Calvin says: they attentively considered the honourable things spoken of them everywhere in Scripture, and as the world is strangely inclined to superstition they obscured the glory of God by extolling angels too much; it was therefore necessary to reduce them to their own rank, that they might not overshadow the brightness of Christ. And first he proves from his name that Christ far excelled them, Calvin says, for he is called the Son of God; some by name understand dignity, but not correctly, as it appears from what follows, for the name by which he is proved here to be superior to angels was that of a Son. That he was distinguished by this title he shows by two testimonies from Scripture, Calvin says, both of which must be examined by us, and then we shall sum up their full import.

Henry takes the objection from the angels and the sense of the participle. The apostle, having proved the pre-eminence of the gospel above the law from the pre-eminence of the Lord Jesus Christ above the prophets, now proceeds to show that he is much superior not only to the prophets but to the angels themselves, Henry says. In this he obviates an objection that the Jewish zealots would be ready to make, that the law was not only delivered by men but ordained by angels, who attended at the giving forth of the law, the hosts of heaven being drawn forth to attend the Lord Jehovah on that awful occasion. Now the angels are very glorious beings, far more glorious and excellent than men, Henry says: the scripture always represents them as the most excellent of all creatures, and we know of no being but God himself that is higher than the angels, and therefore that law that was ordained by angels ought to be held in great esteem. To take off the force of this argument, the penman of this epistle proceeds to state the comparison between Jesus Christ and the holy angels, both in nature and office, and to prove that Christ is vastly superior to the angels themselves. The superior nature of Christ is proved from his superior name, Henry says: the scripture does not give high and glorious titles without a real foundation and reason in nature, nor would such great things have been said of our Lord Jesus Christ if he had not been as great and excellent as those words import. When it is said that Christ was made so much better than the angels we are not to imagine that he was a mere creature, as the angels are, Henry insists: the Greek word, when joined with an adjective, is nowhere to be rendered created, and here may very well be read, being more excellent, as the Syriac version hath it; we read elsewhere, let God be true, not made so, but acknowledged to be so. The superiority of the name and nature of Christ above the angels is declared in the holy scriptures and is to be deduced thence, Henry says: we should have known little or nothing either of Christ or of the angels without the scriptures, and we must therefore be determined by them in our conceptions of the one and the other. Here are several passages of scripture cited in which those things are said of Christ that were never said of the angels, Henry says: it was said of Christ, Thou art my Son, this day have I begotten thee, which may refer to his eternal generation, or to his resurrection, or to his solemn inauguration into his glorious kingdom at his ascension and session at the right hand of the Father, and this was never said concerning the angels, so that by inheritance he has a more excellent nature and name than they. It was said concerning Christ, but never concerning the angels, I will be to him a Father and he shall be to me a Son, Henry says: not only that God is his Father and he his Son by nature and eternal promanation, but that he will be his Father and he shall be his Son by wonderful conception, and this his sonship shall be the fountain and foundation of every gracious relation between God and fallen man.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson take the exaltation, the name and the method of proof. Being made so much better means being exalted so much above the angels, Barnes says: the word better here does not refer to moral character but to exaltation of rank, and as Mediator, as the Son of God in our nature, he is exalted far above all angels of every rank, being exalted to his mediatorial throne with all things placed beneath his feet. By inheritance means in virtue of his name, the Son of God, an exaltation such as is implied in that name, Barnes says: as a son has a rank in a family above servants, as he has a control over the property above that which servants have, so it is with the Mediator, for he is the Son of God while angels are the servants of God and the servants of the church, occupying a place in the universe compared with his such as servants in a family occupy compared with a son. The argument which the apostle insists on is that the title the Son of God is to be given to him alone, Barnes says: it has been conferred on no others, and though the angels and though saints are called in general sons of God, yet that title has been given to him only; and as the apostle was writing to Hebrews he makes his appeal to the Hebrew Scriptures alone for the confirmation of this opinion. A more excellent name means the name Son, Barnes says, a more honourable and exalted name than has ever been bestowed on them, involving more exalted privileges and entitling him on whom it is bestowed to higher respect and honour than any name ever bestowed on them. Ellicott renders being made as having become, and says these words must be closely joined with the last clause of the preceding verse: they speak not of the glory which was ever his but of that which became his after he had made purification of sins. Better means greater, Ellicott says, and we may discern a twofold reason for the comparison, since having become greater than the angels our Lord is exalted above the highest of created beings and above those through whom God had in former time declared his law. The verses which follow show that we are to understand by name all the dignity and glory contained in the name Son of God, Ellicott says: not that this name first belonged to him as exalted Mediator, but the glory which became his is proportionate to and consonant with the name which is his by essential right, and that this name and dignity belong to Jesus Christ, as yet unnamed but confessedly the subject of the preceding verses, is now to be established by the testimony of Scripture. Two important questions have been asked, Ellicott says: does the writer adduce these quotations as strictly demonstrative, and if so, on what assumption does their relevancy rest? It is evident that the whole argument is addressed to men who believed that the Christ had appeared in the person of Jesus, Ellicott answers: of the passages here cited some were already by universal consent applied to the Messiah, and as to the others it was sufficient if the trained and thoughtful reader could recognise the accuracy of such an application when once suggested; in no case is there mere accommodation or illustration, and the writer's object is less to convince his readers of some new truth than to draw attention to what the well-known passages really contain and express. Robertson notes that having become is a second aorist middle participle in contrast with the being of the preceding verse, and that by so much is an instrumental correlative with the as of the second clause, both clauses having comparatives. Hath inherited is a perfect active indicative, Robertson says, and he still inherits it, the name, in the oriental sense of rank, of Son, which is superior to prophets as already shown and also to angels as he now proceeds to prove: Jesus is superior to angels as God's Son, his deity, and the author proves it from Scripture.

Clarke and Wesley take the Jewish estimate of angels and the structure of the argument. So much better than the angels is another argument in favour of the Divinity of our Lord, Clarke says. The Jews had the highest opinion of the transcendent excellence of angels: they even associate them with God in the creation of the world, and suppose them to be of the privy council of the Most High, and thus they understand the words, let us make man in our own image, as spoken by the Lord to the ministering angels that stood before him. They even allow them to be worshipped for the sake of their Creator, and as his representatives, Clarke says, though they will not allow them to be worshipped for their own sake; as, therefore, the Jews considered them next to God, and none entitled to their adoration but God, on their own ground the apostle proves Jesus Christ to be God, because God commanded all the angels of heaven to worship him. He, therefore, who is greater than the angels and is the object of their adoration is God, Clarke argues; but Jesus Christ is greater than the angels and the object of their adoration; therefore Jesus Christ must be God. The verb rendered obtained by inheritance signifies generally to participate, possess, obtain or acquire, and is so used by the purest Greek writers, Clarke says: it is not by inheritance that Christ possesses a more excellent name than angels, but as God he has it naturally and essentially, and as God manifested in the flesh he has it in consequence of his humiliation, sufferings and meritorious death. Wesley says this verse has two clauses, the latter of which is treated of in the next verse and the former at the end of the chapter: such transpositions are also found in the other epistles of Paul, but in none so frequently as in this, the Jewish doctors being peculiarly fond of this figure and using it much in all their writings, so that the apostle, becoming all things to all men, here follows the same method. All the inspired writers were readier in all the figures of speech than the most experienced orators, Wesley adds. Being means by his exaltation, after he had been lower than them, Wesley says, and it was extremely proper to observe that he is so much higher than the angels, because the Jews gloried in their law as it was delivered by the ministration of angels: how much more may we glory in the gospel, which was given not by the ministry of angels but of the very Son of God. Because he is the Son of God he inherits that name, in right whereof he inherits all things, Wesley says: his inheriting that name is more ancient than all worlds, his inheriting all things as ancient as all things; and the angels do not inherit all things, but are themselves a portion of the Son's inheritance, whom they worship as their Lord.

debates: What the participle rendered being made allows. Henry insists that the word joined with an adjective is nowhere to be rendered created and prefers being more excellent, citing the Syriac; Gill says it signifies no more than that he was, and that Christ was made so when he was manifested and declared to be so; Ellicott renders it having become and ties it to the purification of sins in the previous verse, so that it speaks of a glory that became his and was not always his; Robertson marks the same contrast in the Greek; Wesley says simply that it was by his exaltation, after he had been lower than they.

Whether the name is held by inheritance. Wesley says that because he is the Son of God he inherits the name, and dates the inheriting of the name before all worlds and the inheriting of all things as ancient as all things; Clarke denies the word, holding that Christ possesses the name not by inheritance but as God, naturally and essentially, and as God manifested in the flesh in consequence of his humiliation and death; Robertson notes only that the perfect tense means he inherited and still inherits it.

What name means here. Calvin says that some understand dignity by it, but not correctly, since what follows shows the name to be that of a Son; Robertson glosses it as name in the oriental sense of rank; Barnes and Ellicott agree that the name is Son, Barnes adding that although angels and saints are called sons of God in general, the title the Son of God is given to him alone.

How the coming quotations are meant to work. Ellicott raises the question whether they are adduced as strictly demonstrative, and answers that the argument is addressed to men who already believed the Christ had appeared in Jesus, some passages being applied to the Messiah by universal consent and the rest recognisable once suggested, so that the writer's object is less to convince of a new truth than to draw attention to what the passages really contain; the others simply take the citations in turn.
outliers: Clarke alone casts the argument as a formal syllogism, that he who is greater than the angels and is the object of their adoration is God, that Jesus Christ is both, and therefore that Jesus Christ must be God, and grounds it on the Jews' own estimate of angels.

Wesley alone notices the shape of the argument, that the verse has two clauses of which the second is taken up immediately and the first only at the end of the chapter, and identifies the transposition as a figure the Jewish doctors were fond of, which the apostle adopts in becoming all things to all men.

Clarke alone reports that the Jews allowed angels to be worshipped for their Creator's sake, as his representatives, while refusing them worship for their own sake, and uses that concession as the hinge of his argument.

Gill alone answers the comparison with a ladder of ranks rather than an exegesis, setting Creator above creature, the blesser above the blessed, the worshipped above the worshipper, and the sender above the sent.
