5.pericope_label: For unto which of the angels said he at any time, Thou art my Son, this day have I begotten thee? And again, I will be to him a Father, and he shall be to me a Son?

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin take the exclusiveness of the title and the objection from other sons. Gill says that unto which of the angels said he at any time means that he never said to any of the angels what he has said to Christ. Calvin says it cannot be denied but that this was spoken of David, that is, as he sustained the person of Christ: the things found in this Psalm must have been shadowed forth in David but were fully accomplished in Christ. For that he by subduing many enemies around him enlarged the borders of his kingdom was some foreshadowing of the promise, I will give thee the heathen for thine inheritance, Calvin says, but how little was this in comparison with the amplitude of Christ's kingdom, which extends from the east to the west. For the same reason David was called the son of God, having been especially chosen to perform great things, but his glory was hardly a spark, even the smallest, to that glory which shone forth in Christ, on whom the Father has imprinted his own image; so the name of Son belongs by a peculiar privilege to Christ alone and cannot in this sense be applied to any other without profanation. But still the argument of the Apostle seems not to be well-grounded, Calvin objects: how does he maintain that Christ is superior to angels except on this ground, that he has the name of a Son, as though he had not this in common with princes and those high in power, of whom it is written, Ye are gods and the sons of the Most High, and as though Jeremiah had not spoken as honourably of all Israel when he called them the firstborn of God? Besides, David calls angels the sons of God, saying, Who is like to Jehovah among the sons of God? The answer to all this is in no way difficult, Calvin replies: princes are called by this name on account of a particular circumstance; as to Israel, the common grace of election is thus denoted; angels are called the sons of God as having a certain resemblance to him, because they are celestial spirits and possess some portion of divinity in their blessed immortality. But when David, without any addition, calls himself as the type of Christ the Son of God, Calvin says, he denotes something peculiar and more excellent than the honour given to angels or to princes or even to all Israel; otherwise it would have been an improper and absurd expression, if he was by way of excellence called the son of God and yet had nothing more than others, for he is thus separated from all other beings. When it is said so exclusively of Christ, Thou art my Son, it follows that this honour does not belong to any of the angels. If any one again objects and says that David was thus raised above the angels, Calvin answers that it is nothing strange for him to be elevated above angels while bearing the image of Christ.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson take the method of the citation, the first sense of the Psalm and the exclusiveness of the title. The object of this is to prove that the Son of God who has spoken to men in these last days is superior to the angels, Barnes says, and as the apostle was writing to those trained in the Jewish religion, who admitted the authority of the Old Testament, he made his appeal to that and referred for proof to those places generally admitted to relate to the Messiah; it was the common opinion of the Jewish doctors, one authority says, that the Messiah would be exalted above Abraham, Moses and the angels. There is a difficulty in applying the passages which follow to the Messiah, Barnes admits, a difficulty which we may find it not easy to explain. In general it may be observed that it is to be presumed that these passages were, in the time of Paul, applied to the Messiah, since he seems to argue from them as though this was commonly understood and is at no pains to prove it; that it is to be presumed that those to whom he wrote would at once admit this to be so, since otherwise we cannot suppose he would regard this mode of reasoning as adapted to convince them; that he did not apprehend that his application of these texts would be called in question by the countrymen of those to whom he wrote; and that Paul, having been instructed in early life in the doctrines of the Jewish religion and made fully acquainted with all their principles of interpretation, made these quotations in accordance with the prevalent belief and with principles well understood and admitted. Every age and people have their own modes of reasoning, Barnes says: they may differ from others, and others may regard them as unsound, and yet, to that age and people, they are satisfactory and conclusive. The ancient philosophers employed modes of reasoning which would not strike us as the most forcible, and which perhaps we should not regard as tenable; so it is with the Chinese, the Hindoos, the Mohammedans now; so it was with the writers of the dark ages, who lived under the influence of the scholastic philosophy, and they argue from admitted principles in their country and time, just as we do in ours, their reasoning being as satisfactory to them as ours is to us. In a writer of any particular age we are to expect to find the prevailing mode of reasoning and appeals to the usual arguments on any subject, Barnes says: we are not to look for methods of argument founded on the inductive philosophy in the writings of the schoolmen or in the writings of the Chinese or the Hindoos, since it would be unreasonable to expect it; we are to expect that they will be found to reason in accordance with the customs of their time, to appeal to such arguments as were commonly alleged, and, if they are reasoning with an adversary, to make use of the points which he concedes and to urge them as fitted to convince him. And this is not wrong, Barnes concludes. Ellicott paraphrases the argument thus, that God has spoken of the Messiah as his Son, a title which no angel ever receives from him; that the appellation sons of God may be used in an inferior sense, and that thus angels may be so designated, does not affect this argument, for every reader must perceive that in these quotations Son is used of One, and in a sense that is unique. The two quotations are taken from the second Psalm and from the second book of Samuel, Ellicott says, and it seems probable that the Psalm was written by David during the troublous times that followed, in the fresh recollection of the promises recorded there: in the midst of the rebellious conspiracies of kings and nations is heard Jehovah's word, Yet have I set my King upon my holy hill of Zion, and the Anointed King declares the divine decree, The Lord hath said unto me, Thou art my Son, this day have I begotten thee. The clearest comments are supplied by the passage in Samuel, and especially by the eighty-ninth Psalm, where the words I will make him my firstborn, higher than the kings of the earth, show plainly that in their first meaning, that which relates to the royal rule of David or David's son, the words I have this day begotten thee signify, I have this day established thee as my chosen king and thus constituted thee my son, for to the firstborn belongs natural, though derived, rule over the kingdom of his father. At what period the people in general learnt in how secondary a sense such words could be used of any human king we do not know, Ellicott says, but we have clear evidence both from the New Testament and from Jewish tradition that the second Psalm was understood to be a distinct prophecy of the Messiah; indeed, this very name Messiah and the appellation Son of God may be traced to this Psalm. Paul refers the words here quoted to the period of the Resurrection, Ellicott says, and with this the language used in the previous verse perfectly agrees; as, however, in that verse the exaltation of the Christ is declared to correspond to that essential dignity which lay in the name Son, a name which in this very context bears its highest sense, we are constrained to regard the day of the Resurrection as itself typical, and to believe that this day also pointed to the eternal Now, to what an early father speaks of as the day which is co-extensive with the unbegotten and everlasting life of God. The second passage, which seems to have been the basis of the words we have just considered, occurs in the course of the divine promise that David's seed shall be established in his kingdom and that David's throne shall be established for ever, Ellicott says, and with the words here quoted are closely joined others which plainly prove that this is not a simple and direct prophecy of Christ but in the first instance belonged to an earthly ruler. Robertson says the question is, to which individual angel: as a class angels are called sons of God, but no single angel is called God's Son like the Messiah in the second Psalm. A scholar takes have I begotten thee, a perfect active indicative, to refer to the resurrection and ascension, while others refer it to the incarnation, Robertson notes. The second quotation is from the second book of Samuel, and the preposition in the predicate has the sense of as, a Greek rendering of the Hebrew idiom not preserved in the English; the same passage is applied elsewhere to the relation between God and Christians, while here it is treated as Messianic.

Clarke and Wesley take the day of the begetting. The words Thou art my Son, this day have I begotten thee are quoted from the second Psalm, a psalm that seems to refer only to the Messiah, Clarke says, and they are quoted by Paul as referring to the resurrection of Christ, an application confirmed by the same apostle where he says that by his resurrection from the dead he was declared, manifestly proved, to be the Son of God with power, God having put forth his miraculous energy in raising that body from the grave which had truly died, and died a violent death; for Christ was put to death as a malefactor, but by his resurrection his innocence was demonstrated, as God could not work a miracle to raise a wicked man from the dead. As Adam was created by God and was for that reason called the son of God, and could never have seen corruption if he had not sinned, so the human nature of Jesus Christ, formed by the energy of the eternal Spirit in the womb of the virgin without any human intervention, was for this very reason called the Son of God, Clarke says, and because it had not sinned it could not see corruption. The words this day have I begotten thee must refer either to his incarnation, when he was miraculously conceived, or to his resurrection from the dead, when God by this sovereign display of his almighty energy declared him to be his Son, vindicated his innocence, and also the purity of the blessed virgin. The resurrection of Christ, therefore, to which the words most properly refer, not only gave the fullest proof that he was an innocent and righteous man, Clarke says, but also that he had accomplished the purpose for which he died, and that his conception was miraculous and his mother a pure and unspotted virgin. This is a subject of infinite importance to the Christian system and of the last consequence in reference to the conviction and conversion of the Jews, Clarke says: here is the rock on which they split, for they deny this divine Sonship of Jesus Christ, and the certainty of the resurrection of Jesus refutes their every calumny, proves his miraculous conception, vindicates the blessed virgin, and declares him to be the Son of God with power. This most important use of this saying has passed unnoticed by almost every Christian writer which I have seen, Clarke adds, and yet it lies here at the foundation of all the apostle's proofs; if Jesus was not thus the Son of God, the whole Christian system is vain and baseless. Wesley says, Thou art my Son, God of God, Light of Light; this day have I begotten thee means, I have begotten thee from eternity, which, by its unalterable permanency of duration, is one continued, unsuccessive day. I will be to him a Father, and he shall be to me a Son, Wesley says, means, I will own myself to be his Father, and him to be my Son, by eminent tokens of my peculiar love: the former clause relates to his natural Sonship, by an eternal, inconceivable generation, the other to his Father's acknowledgment and treatment of him as his incarnate Son; and indeed this promise related immediately to Solomon, but in a far higher sense to the Messiah.

Cyril takes the Jewish refusal of the Father's name. For thus shall we raise our thoughts higher than the Jews, Cyril says, who admit indeed by their doctrines that there is One God, though what if they often denied even this by their idolatries; but that he is also the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ they admit not, being of a contrary mind to their own Prophets, who in the Divine Scriptures affirm, The Lord said unto me, Thou art My Son, this day have I begotten thee. And to this day they rage and gather themselves together against the Lord and against his Anointed, Cyril says, thinking that it is possible to be made friends of the Father apart from devotion towards the Son, being ignorant that no man cometh unto the Father but by the Son, who saith, I am the Door, and I am the Way. He therefore that refuseth the Way which leadeth to the Father, and he that denieth the Door, how shall he be deemed worthy of entrance unto God? Cyril asks. They contradict also what is written in the Psalm, He shall call me, Thou art my Father, my God, and the helper of my salvation.

debates: When this day was. Clarke says the words must refer either to the incarnation or to the resurrection and decides for the resurrection, on which he then builds a proof of Christ's innocence and of the virgin birth; Wesley refers them to eternity, which by its unalterable permanency of duration is one continued, unsuccessive day; Ellicott grants the reference to the Resurrection but regards that day as itself typical, pointing to the eternal Now; Robertson reports the division without deciding.

How the objection from other sons of God is met. Calvin states it at its strongest, that princes, Israel and the angels are all called sons of God, and answers that each is so called for a particular reason while David as the type of Christ is called Son without addition and so separated from all other beings; Ellicott says the inferior use does not affect the argument, since Son is here used of One and in a unique sense; Robertson makes the whole point turn on the singular, that no individual angel is ever called God's Son.

How far the words belonged first to an earthly king. Calvin says the Psalm was spoken of David as he sustained the person of Christ, shadowed forth in him and fully accomplished in Christ; Ellicott gives the first sense as an enthronement formula, I have this day established thee as my chosen king, and says the second quotation is not a simple and direct prophecy of Christ but belonged in the first instance to an earthly ruler; Wesley says the promise related immediately to Solomon but in a far higher sense to the Messiah.

Whether the citations prove what they are made to prove. Barnes admits a difficulty in applying the passages to the Messiah which we may find it not easy to explain, and defends the argument by the reception it would have had rather than by exegesis, adding that every age has its own modes of reasoning which are conclusive to it though not to us; Ellicott had answered the same question at the previous verse by the readers' prior belief; the rest take the citations as they stand.
outliers: Barnes alone concedes that the apostle's mode of argument may not be ours, comparing it to the reasoning of the ancient philosophers, the schoolmen, and the Chinese, the Hindoos and the Mohammedans of his own day, and concluding that to reason from an adversary's own concessions is not wrong.

Clarke alone turns the verse into an apologetic against Jewish objections, arguing that the resurrection proves Christ innocent, since God could not raise a wicked man by miracle, and thereby vindicates his mother, and complaining that this use of the saying has passed unnoticed by almost every Christian writer he has seen.
Cyril alone is still addressing the adversary rather than describing him, asking how one who refuses the Way that leads to the Father and denies the Door shall be deemed worthy of entrance unto God.
Wesley alone defines the day itself, calling eternity one continued, unsuccessive day by its unalterable permanency of duration.

6.pericope_label: And again, when he bringeth in the firstbegotten into the world, he saith, And let all the angels of God worship him. And of the angels he saith, Who maketh his angels spirits, and his ministers a flame of fire.

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin take the firstbegotten and the application of the psalm. By the firstbegotten is meant Christ, Gill says: this is a name given him in the Old Testament and is what the Hebrews were acquainted with, and therefore the apostle uses it, and the ancient Jews acknowledge the passage from which it seems to be taken is to be understood of the Messiah. As the Son of God he is the only begotten of the Father and was begotten from eternity, before any creature had a being, and therefore called the firstborn of every creature, Gill says, and is sometimes styled the first begotten from the dead, since he rose the first in time and is the first in causality and dignity; he may also be called the firstborn with respect to the saints, who are of the same nature with him and are adopted into the family of God, though they are not in the same class of sonship with him. The bringing of him into the world may refer to his second coming, Gill says, for this seems agreeable from the natural order of the words. On the next verse Gill notes that the phrase means to the angels, or of them, as in the following verse, to the Son, which stands opposed to this. Calvin says the Apostle now proves by another argument that Christ is above the angels, and that is because the angels are bidden to worship him, whence it follows that he is their head and Prince. But it may seem unreasonable to apply that to Christ which is spoken of God only, Calvin says: were we to answer that Christ is the eternal God, and therefore what belongs to God may justly be applied to him, it would not perhaps be satisfactory to all, for it would avail but little in proving a doubtful point to argue in this case from the common attributes of God. The subject is Christ manifested in the flesh, and the Apostle expressly says that the Spirit thus spoke when Christ was introduced into the world, Calvin says, but this would not have been said consistently with truth except the manifestation of Christ be really spoken of in the Psalm; and so the case indeed is, for the Psalm commences with an exhortation to rejoice, nor did David address the Jews but the whole earth, including the islands, that is, countries beyond the sea. If you read the whole Psalm you will find nothing else but the kingdom of Christ, which began when the Gospel was published, Calvin says, nor is the whole Psalm anything else but a solemn decree, as it were, by which Christ was sent to take possession of his kingdom; and what joy could arise from his kingdom except it brought salvation to the whole world, to the Gentiles as well as to the Jews? Aptly then does the Apostle say here that he was introduced into the world, because in that Psalm what is described is his coming to men. The Hebrew word rendered angels is gods, Calvin notes, but there is no doubt that the Prophet speaks of angels, for the meaning is that there is no power so high but must be in subjection to the authority of this king. On the next verse Calvin says the passage quoted seems to have been turned to another meaning from what it appears to have, for as David is there describing the manner in which we see the world to be governed, nothing is more certain than that the winds are mentioned, which he says are made messengers by the Lord, for he employs them as his runners; so also, when he purifies the air by lightnings, he shows what quick and swift ministers he has to obey his orders. But this has nothing to do with angels, Calvin says. Some have had recourse to an allegory, as though the Apostle explained the plain and literal sense allegorically of angels, but it seems preferable to me to consider this testimony as brought forward for this purpose, that it might by a similitude be applied to angels, and in this way David compares winds to angels, because they perform offices in this world similar to what the angels do in heaven, for the winds are, as it were, visible spirits. And doubtless, as Moses, describing the creation of the world, mentioned only those things which are subject to our senses and yet intended that higher things should be understood, so David in describing the world and nature represented to us on a tablet what ought to be understood respecting the celestial orders; hence I think that the argument is one of likeness or similarity, Calvin says, when the Apostle transfers to angels what properly applies to the winds.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson take the word again, the source of the quotation and the rendering of the next verse. The word again refers not to the fact that the Son of God is brought again into the world, implying that he had been introduced before, Barnes says, but to the course of the apostle's argument, or to the declaration made about the Messiah in another place: the name Son is not only given to him as above but also in another place. When he bringeth in means when he introduces, and so far as the language here is concerned this might refer to the birth of the Messiah, Barnes says, but it is evident from the whole connexion that the writer meant to refer to something said in the Old Testament, since the passage occurs among quotations designed to prove a specific point, that the Son of God was superior to the angels: a declaration of the writer here, however true and solemn, would not have answered the purpose, for a proof-text was wanting. The meaning then is that on another occasion God, when speaking of the Messiah, or when introducing him to mankind, had used language showing that he was superior to the angels, Barnes says. Christ is called the firstbegotten with reference to his resurrection from the dead elsewhere, but it is probable here that the word is used, like firstborn among the Hebrews, by way of eminence: as the firstborn was the principal heir and had peculiar privileges, so the Lord Jesus Christ sustains a similar rank in the universe of which God is the Head and Father. Much difficulty has been experienced in regard to this quotation, Barnes says, for it cannot be denied that it is intended to be a quotation: in the Septuagint these very words occur at the end of the Song of Moses, where they are inserted, but they are not in the Hebrew, nor are they in all the copies of the Septuagint. On the next verse Barnes says he gives to the angels an inferior name and assigns them a more humble office: they are mere ministers and have not ascribed to them the name of Son, but a name which implies a more humble rank and office, and they obey his will as the winds and the lightnings do. The object of the apostle is to show that the angels serve God in a ministerial capacity, as the winds do, while the Son is Lord of all, Barnes says: the one serves him passively, as being wholly under his control, the other acts as a Sovereign. The passage might be translated, who maketh his angels winds and his ministers a flame of fire, that is, who makes his angels as swift as the winds and his ministers as rapid and as resistless as the lightning. The passage in the Psalm is susceptible of another interpretation, Barnes says, and might be regarded as meaning, who makes the winds his messengers and the flaming fire his ministers, and perhaps this is the sense which would most naturally occur to a reader of the Hebrew; the Hebrew, however, will admit of the construction here put upon it, and it cannot be proved that it was the original intention of the passage to show that the angels were the mere servants of God. It is to be presumed that Paul, who had been trained in the knowledge of the Hebrew language, would have had a better opportunity of knowing its fair construction than we can, Barnes adds, and it is morally certain that he would employ the passage in an argument as it was commonly understood by those to whom he wrote. Ellicott says there seems little doubt that the true translation is, And when he again leadeth the Firstborn into the world he saith: the position of again in the Greek shows that it does not indicate a new step in the argument but must be joined with leadeth, and the speaker is God, speaking in the word of Scripture. The quotation involves some difficulty, Ellicott says: it cannot be directly taken from the ninety-seventh Psalm, for the citations from the Greek Bible in this Epistle are usually so exact that we cannot believe the writer would have so altered the form of the sentence; in the Song of Moses, however, we find words identical with those of the text in most copies of the Greek, but there is nothing answering to them in the Hebrew, and there is no sufficient reason for supposing that the clause has dropped out of the Hebrew text. There are similarities both of subject and of diction between the Psalm and the last section of the Song, Ellicott says, which make it easy to see how the words could find their way into the Song; the Psalm belongs to a cycle whose theme is the triumphant announcement of the coming of God's kingdom, by which was denoted the kingdom of Christ, and in both Psalm and Song we read of the judgment exercised and the vengeance inflicted by the enthroned King. When the Messiah, reigning as the Firstborn of God, shall appear for judgment, that is, when God leadeth a second time his Firstborn into the world of men, that he may receive full possession of his inheritance, he saith, And let all angels of God worship him. On the next verse Ellicott says spirits is better rendered winds: it is very difficult to assign any clear meaning to the ordinary rendering, and the parallelism in these two lines of Hebrew poetry is complete, angels answering to ministers and winds to a flame of fire. The meaning appears to be that God, employing his messengers for his varied purposes, sends them forth in what manner he may please, clothing them with the appearance of the resistless wind or the devouring fire, Ellicott says, and the force of the passage lies in the vividness with which it presents the thought of the Most High served by angels untiring as the wind and subtle as the fire. Whether this translation faithfully represents the original is a question that has been warmly discussed, Ellicott adds: it is often alleged that the context requires an inversion of the words, who maketh winds his messengers, flaming fire his ministers, and the point cannot be examined here, but he expresses a decided opinion that the translation defended above not only expresses the meaning of the Hebrew but perfectly accords with the context of the Psalm. Robertson says the clause is an indefinite temporal one, and that if again is taken with the verb the reference is to the Second Coming, while if again merely introduces another quotation parallel to the and again of the previous verse, the reference is to the incarnation, when the angels did worship the Child Jesus; there is no way to decide certainly about it. The world means the inhabited earth, and the imperative is here in the full sense of worship, not mere reverence or courtesy, Robertson says: this quotation is from the Greek of the Song of Moses but is not in the Hebrew, though most manuscripts have sons of God, and the substance does occur also in the ninety-seventh Psalm. On the next verse Robertson notes the balanced contrast of particles between this verse and the next, and that the word rendered spirits also means winds: the meaning apparently is one that can reduce angels to the elemental forces of wind and fire. A scholar holds that the Hebrew here is wrongly rendered and means that God makes the wind his messengers, not angels, and flaming fire his servants, Robertson says: that is all true, but that is not the point of this passage.

Clarke and Wesley take the second bringing in and the nature of angels. This is not a correct translation, Clarke says: it should be, but when he bringeth again, or the second time, the firstborn into the habitable world. This most manifestly refers to his resurrection, which might be properly considered a second incarnation, Clarke argues, for as the human soul as well as the fullness of the Godhead bodily dwelt in the man Christ Jesus during his incarnation, so when he expired upon the cross both the Godhead and the human spirit left his dead body, and as on his resurrection these were reunited to his revivified manhood, therefore with the strictest propriety does the apostle say that the resurrection was a second bringing of him into the world. Clarke distinguishes the two Greek words, translating the one here as the habitable world and noting that the other signifies the terraqueous globe independently of its inhabitants: our Lord's first coming into the world is expressed by the latter word, and this simply refers to his being incarnated that he might be capable of suffering and dying for man, but the word is changed on this second coming, and why? Because he was now to dwell with man, to send his gospel everywhere to all the inhabitants of the earth, and to accompany that Gospel wherever he sent it. The apostle recurs here to his former assertion that Jesus is higher than the angels, Clarke says, that he is none of those who can be called ordinary angels or messengers, but one of the most extraordinary kind, and the object of worship to all the angels of God. To worship any creature is idolatry, and God resents idolatry more than any other evil, Clarke argues: Jesus Christ can be no creature, else the angels who worship him must be guilty of idolatry, and God the author of that idolatry, who commanded those angels to worship Christ. There has been some difficulty in ascertaining the place from which the apostle quotes these words, Clarke says: some suppose the ninety-seventh Psalm, which the Greek renders, Worship him, all ye his angels, but it is not clear that the Messiah is intended in that psalm, nor are the words precisely those used here by the apostle; our marginal references send us with great propriety to the Greek version of the Song of Moses, where the passage is found word for word, but there is nothing answering to the words in the present Hebrew text. On the next verse Clarke says the angels are so far from being superior to Christ that they are not called God's sons in any peculiar sense, but his servants, as tempests and lightnings are; in many respects they may have been made inferior even to man as he came out of the hands of his Maker, for he was made in the image and likeness of God, but of the angels, even the highest order of them, this is never spoken. It is very likely that the apostle refers here to the opinions of the Jews relative to the angels, Clarke says, and he cites their sayings: that the angels created the second day, when they minister before God, become fire; that God is named the Lord of hosts because with his angels he doth whatsoever he wills, making them sit down, or stand, or appear like women, or like men, or making them spirits, or making them fire; and that an angel answered Manoah, I know not in whose image I am made, for God changeth us every hour, sometimes making us fire, sometimes spirit, sometimes men, and at other times angels. It is very probable that those who are termed angels are not confined to any specific form or shape, Clarke concludes, but assume various forms and appearances according to the nature of the work on which they are employed and the will of their sovereign employer, and this seems to have been the ancient Jewish doctrine on the subject. Wesley says the appellation firstbegotten includes that of Son, together with the rights of primogeniture which the firstbegotten Son of God enjoys in a manner not communicable to any creature, and that into the world means at his incarnation: so much higher was he, when in his lowest estate, than the highest angel. On the next verse Wesley says, Who maketh his angels, implies that they are only creatures, whereas the Son is eternal and the Creator himself; and spirits and a flame of fire intimates not only their office but also their nature, which is excellent indeed, the metaphor being taken from the most swift, subtle and efficacious things on earth, but nevertheless infinitely below the majesty of the Son.

Chrysostom and Cyril take the direction of the coming and the senses of the word spirit. Our Lord Jesus Christ calls his coming in the flesh an exodus or going out, Chrysostom says, as when he saith, The sower went out to sow, and again, I went out from the Father and am come; but Paul calls it a coming in, saying, And when again he bringeth in the First-Begotten into the world, meaning by this bringing in his taking on him flesh. Now why has he so used the expression? For Christ indeed calls it a going out, justly, for we were out from God, Chrysostom says: as in royal palaces prisoners and those who have offended the king stand without, and he who desires to reconcile them does not bring them in, but himself going out discourses with them, until, having made them meet for the king's presence, he may bring them in, so also Christ hath done, having gone out to us, that is, having taken flesh, and having discoursed to us of the King's matters, so he brought us in, having purged the sins and made reconciliation. But Paul names it a coming in, from the metaphor of those who come to an inheritance and receive any portion or possession, Chrysostom says: for the saying, when again he bringeth in the First-Begotten into the world, means this, when he putteth the world into his hand; for when he was made known, then also he obtained possession of the whole thereof. He saith not these things concerning God the Word, Chrysostom adds, but concerning that which is according to the flesh. Cyril says that since concerning spirit in general many diverse things are written in the divine Scriptures, and there is fear lest some out of ignorance fall into confusion, not knowing to what sort of spirit the writing refers, it will be well now to certify you of what kind the Scripture declares the Holy Spirit to be. For as Aaron is called Christ, and David and Saul and others are called Christs, but there is only one true Christ, so likewise, since the name of spirit is given to different things, it is right to see what is that which is distinctively called the Holy Spirit, Cyril says. For many things are called spirits: thus an Angel is called spirit, our soul is called spirit, and this wind which is blowing is called spirit; great virtue also is spoken of as spirit, and impure practice is called spirit, and a devil our adversary is called spirit. Beware therefore when thou hearest these things, Cyril warns, lest from their having a common name thou mistake one for another.

debates: When the bringing in of the Firstborn happens. Barnes says again refers not to a second bringing but to the course of the argument, meaning in another place; Ellicott says the position of the word in the Greek forbids that and joins it to the verb, reading a second leading in for judgment; Clarke calls the rendering incorrect and refers it to the resurrection, which he treats as a second incarnation; Gill also takes it of the second coming; Wesley takes it of the incarnation; Robertson lays out both chief options and says there is no way to decide certainly.

Whether the verse should read spirits or winds. Ellicott says winds, since the ordinary rendering yields no clear meaning and the parallelism is complete, and records a decided opinion against the proposed inversion; Barnes allows that the inverted sense, who makes the winds his messengers, is perhaps what would most naturally occur to a reader of the Hebrew; Calvin says the Psalm is about winds and has nothing to do with angels, the Apostle arguing by likeness since the winds are as it were visible spirits; Robertson grants that the inversion is all true but denies that it is the point here; Wesley keeps spirits and takes the word of their nature as well as their office.

Where the quotation comes from. Barnes, Clarke, Ellicott and Robertson agree that the words stand word for word in the Greek of the Song of Moses and not at all in the Hebrew, Clarke and Ellicott adding that the ninety-seventh Psalm cannot be the source since its wording differs; Ellicott holds there is no sufficient reason to suppose the clause dropped out of the Hebrew; Calvin cites the Psalm as the source and raises no difficulty at all.

How the angels may be commanded to worship him. Clarke argues that to worship a creature is idolatry, so that if Christ were a creature God would be the author of the angels' idolatry; Calvin refuses to argue from the common attributes of God, since that would avail little in a doubtful point, and argues instead that the whole Psalm describes the kingdom of Christ; Wesley says only that so much higher was he in his lowest estate than the highest angel.
outliers: Chrysostom alone asks why the coming is called a going out by Christ and a coming in by Paul, and answers with the picture of the king's palace, where the offenders stand outside and the reconciler goes out to talk with them until they are fit to be brought in.

Cyril alone, drawn here by the single word spirit, enumerates its senses in Scripture, an angel, the soul, the wind that is blowing, great virtue, impure practice and the devil, and warns the hearer not to mistake one for another because they share a name.

Clarke alone presses the difference between two Greek words for world, arguing that the first coming is described by the word for the globe and this by the word for the inhabited earth, because now he was to dwell with man.

Clarke alone collects the rabbinic sayings about the mutability of angels, including the answer given to Manoah, that the angel did not know in whose image he was made, since God changed them every hour.

let all the angels of God worship him

who maketh his angels spirits

8.pericope_label: But unto the Son he saith, Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever: a sceptre of righteousness is the sceptre of thy kingdom.

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin take the address to the Son and the vocative. Gill says that what he says unto the Son he does not say to angels, which sets him infinitely above them, and which shows him to be a Prince and King and not a servant or minister, and which even ascribes deity to him. Calvin says it must indeed be allowed that this Psalm was composed as a marriage song for Solomon, for here is celebrated his marriage with the daughter of the king of Egypt, but it cannot yet be denied that what is here related is much too high to be applied to Solomon. The Jews, that they may not be forced to own Christ to be called God, make an evasion by saying that the throne of God is spoken of, or that the verb established is to be understood, Calvin says: so that according to the first exposition the word Elohim, God, is to be in construction with throne, the throne of God, and according to the second the sentence is supposed to be defective. But these are mere evasions, Calvin replies: whosoever will read the verse, who is of a sound mind and free from the spirit of contention, cannot doubt but that the Messiah is called God. Nor is there any reason to object that the word Elohim is sometimes given to angels and to judges, Calvin adds, for it is never found to be given simply to one person except to God alone. Further, that I may not contend about a word, whose throne can be said to be established except that of God only? Hence the perpetuity of his kingdom is an evidence of his divinity. The sceptre of Christ's kingdom is afterwards called the sceptre of righteousness, Calvin says, of which there were some, though obscure, lineaments in Solomon, who exhibited them as far as he acted as a just king and zealous for what was right; but righteousness in the kingdom of Christ has a wider meaning, for he by his gospel, which is his spiritual sceptre, renews us after the righteousness of God, and the same must be understood of his love of righteousness, for he causes it to reign in his own people because he loves it.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson take the reference of the psalm, its text and the ambiguity of the Greek. The fact that the writer of this epistle makes this application of the Psalm to the Messiah proves that it was so applied in his time, or that it would be readily admitted to be applicable to him, Barnes says, and it has been generally admitted by both Jewish and Christian interpreters to have such a reference: even those who have doubted its primary applicability to the Messiah have regarded it as referring to him in a secondary sense, and many have supposed that it referred to Solomon in the primary sense. To me it seems most probable that it had an original and exclusive reference to the Messiah, Barnes says. It is to be remembered that the hope of the Messiah was the peculiar hope of the Jewish people, and the coming of the future King was the great event to which they all looked forward with the deepest interest: that hope inspired their prophets and their bards and cheered the hearts of the nation in the time of despondency. The Messiah, if I may so express it, was the hero of the Old Testament, Barnes says, more so than Achilles is of the Iliad and Aeneas of the Aeniad: the sacred poets were accustomed to employ all their most magnificent imagery in describing him, and everything that is gorgeous and splendid in description is lavished on him, they being never under any apprehension of attributing to him too great magnificence or too great an extent of dominion. That the description may have been in part derived from the view of Solomon in the magnificence of his court is possible, Barnes allows, but no more probable than that it was derived from the general view of the splendour of any oriental monarch. Indeed, I see not why this Psalm should ever have been supposed to be applicable to Solomon, Barnes says: his name is not mentioned, it has no peculiar applicability to him, and there is nothing that would apply to him which would not also apply to many an oriental prince, while there are some things in it which are much less applicable to him than to many others. The king here described is a conqueror, Barnes argues: he girds his sword on his thigh, and his arrows are sharp in the hearts of his foes, and the people are subdued under him; this was not true of Solomon, whose was a reign of peace and tranquillity, nor was he ever distinguished for war. On the whole it seems clear that this Psalm is designed to be a beautiful poetic description of the Messiah as king. Ellicott says unto is rather of, since the connection with the previous verse is so close that we must not vary the rendering of the preposition. As the words stand in the ordinary Greek text they agree exactly with the Septuagint, Ellicott says, but certain alterations of reading are required by the best evidence: after the words for ever and ever a connecting word must be restored, and in the following clause two words must change places, while a third reading is of much greater importance, for at the close of the verse the two oldest of our Greek manuscripts agree in reading his kingdom. We have every reason to believe that the application of this Psalm which is here made was fully received by the ancient Jews, Ellicott says, since in the Targum on the Psalm the verse is taken as a direct address to the King Messiah, and hence the readers of this Epistle would at once recognise the argument which the words contain. It is strongly maintained by some that the Psalm is altogether prophetic, the promised Messiah alone being in the Psalmist's thought, Ellicott says, but there appear to be insuperable objections to this view, from particular expressions used and from the general structure and colouring of the Psalm. It is in every way more probable that the second Psalm rather than the hundred and tenth represents the class to which this belongs, Ellicott argues: originally writing in celebration of the marriage of a king of David's line, we know not whom, though many of the arguments urged against the possible reference to Solomon have no great weight, the inspired Psalmist uses words which bear their full meaning only when applied to that Son of David of whose kingdom there shall be no end. The promises made to David are before the writer's mind in the first verses of the Psalm, Ellicott says: the king appointed by God is his representative to God's people, his cause is that of truth and righteousness, his dominion will continually advance; and it is at this moment that, with the promise of a divine sonship in his thought, he suddenly addresses the king as Elohim, a divine king who receives from God the reward of righteousness. There are in the Old Testament examples of the use of Elohim which diminish the difficulty of its application to an earthly king, Ellicott grants, but it must still be acknowledged that the passage stands alone, though this difficulty relates only to the primary application, since as the higher and true reference of the words became revealed all earthly limitations disappeared. Robertson says this fifth quotation is from a Hebrew nuptial ode for a king, treated here as Messianic, and that it is not certain whether the word for God is here the vocative, an address with the nominative form as elsewhere with the Messiah termed God, or whether it is nominative, subject or predicate, with is understood, giving either God is thy throne or Thy throne is God: either makes good sense, Robertson says. Sceptre is an old word for a walking-stick or staff.

Clarke and Wesley take the vocative and the singular. If this be said of the Son of God, then Jesus Christ must be God, Clarke says, and indeed the design of the apostle is to prove this. The words quoted are from the forty-fifth Psalm, which the ancient Chaldee paraphrast and the most intelligent rabbins refer to the Messiah, Clarke says: on the third verse of the Psalm the Targum says, Thy beauty, O King Messiah, is greater than the children of men, and a rabbi says, This Psalm speaks of David, or rather of his son, the Messiah, for this is his name; other rabbins confirm this opinion. This verse is very properly considered a proof, and indeed a strong one, of the Divinity of Christ, Clarke says, but some late versions of the New Testament have endeavoured to avoid the evidence of this proof by translating the words thus, God is thy throne for ever and ever; and if this version be correct, it is certain the text can be no proof of the doctrine. One writer vindicates this translation at large, the nominative case being supposed a sufficient justification of the version. In answer to this it may be stated that the nominative case is often used for the vocative, particularly by the Attics, Clarke says, and the whole scope of the place requires it should be so used here; and, with due deference to all of a contrary opinion, the original Hebrew cannot be consistently translated any other way. To this our Lord seems to refer where he says, All power is given unto me, both in heaven and earth, Clarke adds: my throne, that is, my dominion, extends from the creation to the consummation of all things. None of the ancient versions has understood it in the way contended for by those who deny the Godhead of Christ, either in the Psalm from which it is taken or in this place where it is quoted, Clarke says: one early translator renders the word by the vocative, and the Arabic adds the sign of the vocative, reading the place the same as in our version; and even allowing that the word here is to be taken as the nominative case, it will not make the sense contended for without adding a verb to it, a reading which is not countenanced by any version, nor by any manuscript yet discovered. Wesley says that God, in the singular number, is never in scripture used absolutely of any but the supreme God, and that thy reign, of which the sceptre is the ensign, is full of justice and equity.

Cyril takes the anointing and applies it to the hearer. For Christ was not anointed by men with oil or material ointment, Cyril says, but the Father, having before appointed him to be the Saviour of the whole world, anointed him with the Holy Ghost, as Peter says, Jesus of Nazareth, whom God anointed with the Holy Ghost. David also the Prophet cried, saying, Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever; a sceptre of righteousness is the sceptre of thy kingdom; thou hast loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, even thy God, hath anointed thee with the oil of gladness above thy fellows. And as Christ was in reality crucified, and buried, and raised, and you are in Baptism accounted worthy of being crucified, buried and raised together with him in a likeness, Cyril says, so is it with the unction also: as he was anointed with an ideal oil of gladness, that is, with the Holy Ghost, called oil of gladness because he is the author of spiritual gladness, so ye were anointed with ointment, having been made partakers and fellows of Christ.

debates: Whether the Greek is a vocative. Clarke says the nominative form is often used for the vocative, that the scope of the place requires it, that the Hebrew admits no other rendering, and that the alternative would need a verb supplied which no version or manuscript countenances; Calvin calls the alternatives mere evasions made lest Christ be owned as God; Wesley argues from the singular number, never used absolutely in scripture of any but the supreme God; Robertson says it is not certain which the word is, and that either reading makes good sense.

Whether the Psalm ever referred to Solomon. Barnes denies it outright, since Solomon's name is not mentioned, nothing in the Psalm peculiarly fits him, and the king described is a conqueror whereas Solomon's reign was peaceful; Ellicott finds insuperable objections to taking the Psalm as wholly prophetic, holds it written for the marriage of some king of David's line, and says many of the arguments urged against a reference to Solomon have no great weight; Calvin allows the marriage of Solomon as the occasion but says what is related is much too high for him; Robertson calls it a nuptial ode treated here as Messianic.

How far the difficulty of calling a king Elohim reaches. Calvin says the word is never given simply to one person except to God alone; Ellicott grants Old Testament examples that diminish the difficulty of applying it to an earthly king, but acknowledges that the passage stands alone, adding that the difficulty touches only the primary application; Wesley denies the difficulty by denying the usage.

What the sceptre of righteousness means. Calvin finds obscure lineaments of it in Solomon as a just king, but says that in Christ's kingdom it is wider, the gospel being his spiritual sceptre by which he renews us after the righteousness of God; Wesley reads it as the ensign of a reign full of justice and equity; Robertson notes only that the Greek word is an old one for a walking-stick.
outliers: Barnes alone reaches for Homer, calling the Messiah the hero of the Old Testament more than Achilles is of the Iliad, and explaining the psalm's extravagance by the sacred poets' freedom to lavish every gorgeous image on him without fear of excess.

Ellicott alone examines the text of the quotation, noting a connecting word to be restored, two words to change places, and the two oldest Greek manuscripts reading his kingdom at the close of the verse.

Cyril alone turns the verse on the reader, arguing that as the hearer is crucified, buried and raised with Christ in the likeness of baptism, so he shares the unction too, having been made a partaker and fellow of Christ.
Clarke alone canvasses the rival translation at length before rejecting it, conceding that if God is thy throne were correct the text could be no proof of the doctrine at all.

the sceptre of righteousness

9.pericope_label: Thou hast loved righteousness, and hated iniquity; therefore God, even thy God, hath anointed thee with the oil of gladness above thy fellows. And, Thou, Lord, in the beginning hast laid the foundation of the earth; and the heavens are the works of thine hands:

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin take the love of righteousness and the application of the second psalm. Christ loves righteous persons and righteous works, faithfulness and integrity, and a just administration of government, Gill says, which has appeared in the whole course of his life on earth, in working out a righteousness for his people and in encouraging righteousness in them; and his love of justice will still more appear at the last day, when he will judge the world in righteousness. He hates iniquity, or unrighteousness as one copy reads, as being contrary to his nature both as God and man and to the righteous law of God, Gill says, which has appeared by his inveighing against it and dehorting from it, by his severity exercised towards delinquents, by his suffering for it and abolishing of it, and by chastising his own people on account of it. On the next verse Gill says the person here addressed as the Lord, and as the Maker of the heavens and the earth, is the same with the Son spoken to before, for the words are a continuation of the speech to him though taken from another psalm; the phrase thou, Lord, answers to O my God there, and where that psalm says of old and this says in the beginning the sense is the same, an old commentator interpreting it at or from the beginning and the Targum paraphrasing it from the beginning that the creatures were created. This shows the eternity of Christ, the Lord, the Creator of the earth, who must exist before the foundation of the world, Gill says, and confutes the notion of the eternity of the world; the founding of the earth shows that it is the lower part of the creation and denotes its stability. Calvin says the words were indeed truly said of Solomon, who was made a king because God had preferred him to his brethren, who were otherwise his equals, being the sons of the king, but this applies more suitably to Christ, who has adopted us as his joint heirs, though not so in our own right. He was anointed above us all, as it was beyond measure, while we, each of us, are anointed according to a limited portion, as he has divided to each of us, Calvin says; besides, he was anointed for our sake, in order that we may all draw out of his fatness, and hence he is the Christ and we are Christians proceeding from him, as a rivulet from a fountain. But as Christ received this unction when in the flesh, Calvin says, he is said to have been anointed by his God, for it would be inconsistent to suppose him inferior to God except in his human nature: he is evidently throughout spoken of in his mediatorial character, and to keep this in view will enable us more fully to understand the chapter. It is more agreeable to this passage to regard the anointing not as that of consecration but as that of refreshment to guests according to a prevailing custom, Calvin says: the word gladness favours this, and also the previous words of the passage, since Christ is addressed as already on his throne and his administration is referred to, and it is on account of his just administration that he is said to have been anointed with the perfuming oil of gladness. On the next verse Calvin says this testimony at first sight may seem to be unfitly applied to Christ, especially in a doubtful matter such as is here handled, for the subject in dispute is not concerning the glory of God but what may be fitly applied to Christ, and there is not in this passage any mention made of Christ, but the majesty of God alone is set forth. I indeed allow that Christ is not named in any part of the Psalm, Calvin says, but it is yet plain that he is so pointed out that no one can doubt but that his kingdom is there avowedly recommended to us; hence all the things which are found there are to be applied to his person, for in none have they been fulfilled but in Christ, such as, Thou shalt arise and have mercy on Sion, that the heathens may fear thy name, and all the kings of the earth thy glory, and again, When the nations shall be gathered together, and the kingdoms, to serve the Lord. Doubtless, in vain shall we seek to find this God through whom the whole world have united in one faith and worship of God, except in Christ, Calvin says. All the other parts of the Psalm exactly suit the person of Christ, such as that he is the eternal God, the creator of heaven and earth, and that perpetuity belongs to him without any change, by which his majesty is raised to the highest elevation and he himself is removed from the rank of all created beings. What David says about the heavens perishing some explain by adding, Were such a thing to happen, as though nothing was affirmed, Calvin says; but what need is there of such a strained explanation, since we know that all creatures are subjected to vanity? For to what purpose is that renovation promised which even the heavens wait for with strong desire, except that they are now verging towards destruction? But the perpetuity of Christ which is here mentioned brings no common comfort to the godly, Calvin adds, as the Psalm at last teaches us, since they shall be partakers of it, inasmuch as Christ communicates himself and what he possesses to his own body.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson take the character described, the rendering of the divine names, and the application of a psalm addressed to Jehovah. Thou hast loved righteousness means thou hast been obedient to the law of God, or holy and upright, Barnes says: nothing can be more truly adapted to express the character of the Lord Jesus, who was holy, harmless, undefiled, who did no sin and in whose mouth no guile was found, but it is with difficulty that this can be applied to Solomon, for assuredly, for a considerable part of his life, this declaration could not well be appropriate to him. It is language prompted by the warm and pious imagination of the Psalmist, describing the future Messiah, Barnes says, and as applied to him is true to the letter. The word even, inserted here by the translators, weakens the force of the expression, Barnes says: this might be translated, O God, thy God hath anointed thee, and so it is rendered by Clarke and others; the Greek will bear this construction as well as the Hebrew, and this is the most natural construction, as it accords with what is just said before, though it is not material which construction is adopted. Anciently kings and priests were consecrated to their office by pouring oil on their heads, Barnes says, and the expression to anoint therefore comes to mean to consecrate to office or to set apart to some public work, which is evidently the meaning in the Psalm. The oil of gladness probably means the perfumed oil that was poured on the head, attended with many expressions of joy and rejoicing, Barnes says: the inauguration of the Messiah as king would be an occasion of rejoicing and triumph, thousands exulting at it as in the coronation of a king. Above thy fellows means above thine associates, that is, above all who sustain the kingly office, Barnes says, and one commentator supposes it refers to angels who might have been associated with the Messiah in the government of the world, but the more natural construction is otherwise. On the next verse Barnes says the word and means, to add another instance, and is connected with the earlier verse, so that unto the Son he saith, Thy throne, and also he saith, Thou Lord. That this is the meaning is apparent, Barnes argues, because the object of the whole quotation is to show the exalted character of the Son of God, and because an address here to Jehovah would be wholly irrelevant: why, in an argument designed to prove that the Son of God was superior to the angels, should the writer break out in an address to Jehovah, in view of the fact that he had laid the foundations of the world? Such is not the manner of Paul, or of any other good writer, Barnes says, and it is clear that the writer here designed to adduce this as applicable to the Messiah; whatever difficulties there may be about the principles on which it is done, there can be no doubt about the design of the writer, since otherwise the quotation is wholly irrelevant and it is inconceivable why it should have been made. The quotation is from a psalm in which there can be no doubt that Jehovah is intended, Barnes says: this is apparent on the face of the Psalm, and particularly because the name Jehovah is introduced and because he is addressed as the Creator of all things and as immutable; no one, on reading the Psalm, ever would doubt that it referred to God, and if the apostle meant to apply it to the Lord Jesus it proves most conclusively that he is divine. It must be admitted that probably few persons, if any, on reading the Psalm would suppose that it referred to the Messiah, Barnes says, but the fact that the apostle thus employs it proves that it was understood in his time to have such a reference, or at least that those to whom he wrote would admit that it had such a reference. Ellicott says the King by divine election has been exalted by divine reward, and that it is possible, but not probable, that the words both here and in the Psalm should be rendered, Therefore, O God, thy God hath anointed thee. Thy fellows in the first application probably points to other earthly kings, Ellicott says. On the next verse he says these verses are linked by the word and with the earlier one, as presenting the second part of the contrast between angels and the Son: as there we read of a divine sovereignty, so here of the work of creation, the power to change all created things, and the divine attribute of changeless existence. This quotation agrees almost exactly with the Greek text as we have it in the Alexandrian manuscript, Ellicott says, except that the words as a garment, not found in the Psalm, must here be added according to our best authorities. The only point of any difficulty in these verses is that the writer discovers a testimony to the supremacy of the Son in words which, as they stand in the Psalm, would appear to be directly addressed to God as Creator, Ellicott says; if, however, the Psalm be examined, it will be found to contain the expression of hopes which in reality were inseparably united with the fulfilment of the Messianic promise, since the Lord shall appear to build up Zion is the Psalmist's theme, and it is to the same Lord that he addresses the words which are quoted here. As in Jesus the Christian Jew saw him who fulfilled all these promises of God to his people, Ellicott concludes, the application of the words of adoration to the same Lord would at once be recognised as true. Robertson says hath anointed thee is a first aorist of the verb from which the verbal Anointed One comes, and that with the oil of gladness is perhaps the festive anointing on occasions of joy; fellows is an old word meaning partners or sharers, found in the New Testament almost only in this Epistle, and the preposition here means beside, beyond, above, by a comparison extending beyond. On the next verse Robertson notes that the word Lord stands in the Greek version and not in the Hebrew, and that this sixth quotation runs through three verses; he notes also the emphatic position of the pronoun thou at the beginning, and says this Messianic Psalm pictures the Son in his creative work and in his final triumph.

Clarke and Wesley take the anointing and the fellows. Thou hast loved righteousness is the characteristic of a just governor, Clarke says: he abhors and suppresses iniquity, he countenances and supports righteousness and truth. The original may be thus translated, Therefore, O God, thy God hath anointed thee, Clarke says, the form of speech being nearly the same as in the preceding verse, but the sense is sufficiently clear if we read, Therefore God, thy God, hath anointed thee. We have often had occasion to remark that anciently kings, priests and prophets were consecrated to their several offices by anointing, and that this signified the gifts and influences of the Divine Spirit, Clarke says, and Christ signifies the Anointed One, the same as the Hebrew Messias, and he is here said to be anointed with the oil of gladness above his fellows. None was ever constituted prophet, priest and king but himself, Clarke argues: some were kings only, prophets only, and priests only; others were kings and priests, or priests and prophets, or kings and prophets; but none had ever the three offices in his own person but Jesus Christ, and none but himself can be a King over the universe, a Prophet to all intelligent beings, and a Priest to the whole human race. Thus he is infinitely exalted beyond his fellows, all that had ever borne the regal, prophetic or sacerdotal offices, Clarke says. Some think that the word fellows refers to believers who are made partakers of the same Spirit but cannot have its infinite plenitude, Clarke reports, but the first sense seems the best; and gladness is used to express the festivities which took place on the inauguration of kings. On the next verse Clarke says this is an address to the Son as the Creator, for this is implied in laying the foundation of the earth, and the heavens, which are the work of his hands, point out his infinite wisdom and skill. Wesley says, Thou hast loved righteousness and hated iniquity, means, thou art infinitely pure and holy; therefore God, who, as thou art Mediator, is thy God, hath anointed thee with the oil of gladness, that is, with the Holy Ghost, the fountain of joy, above thy fellows, that is, above all the children of men. On the next verse Wesley says, Thou, means the same to whom the discourse is addressed in the preceding verse.

Cyril takes the anointing and the greatness of the Creator. Christ was not anointed by men with oil or material ointment, Cyril says, but the Father, having before appointed him to be the Saviour of the whole world, anointed him with the Holy Ghost; and David also the Prophet cried, saying, Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever, a sceptre of righteousness is the sceptre of thy kingdom, thou hast loved righteousness and hated iniquity, therefore God, even thy God, hath anointed thee with the oil of gladness above thy fellows. As he was anointed with an ideal oil of gladness, that is, with the Holy Ghost, called oil of gladness because he is the author of spiritual gladness, so ye were anointed with ointment, Cyril tells his hearers, having been made partakers and fellows of Christ. On the next verse Cyril says this Father of our Lord Jesus Christ is not circumscribed in any place, nor is he less than the heaven, but the heavens are the works of his fingers and the whole earth is held in his grasp: he is in all things and around all. Think not that the sun is brighter than he, or equal to him, Cyril says, for he who at first formed the sun must needs be incomparably greater and brighter; he foreknoweth the things that shall be, and is mightier than all, knowing all things and doing as he will, not being subject to any necessary sequence of events, nor to nativity, nor chance, nor fate, in all things perfect, and equally possessing every absolute form of virtue, neither diminishing nor increasing, but in mode and conditions ever the same.

debates: Who the fellows are. Clarke takes them for all who ever held the anointed offices, none but Christ having held all three of prophet, priest and king in his own person, and reports but rejects the reading that makes them believers; Calvin holds that rejected reading, that Christ was anointed above us all beyond measure while each of us has a limited portion, so that he is the Christ and we Christians proceeding from him as a rivulet from a fountain, and Cyril says the same to his hearers; Ellicott takes them in the first application for other earthly kings and Barnes for all who sustain the kingly office, reporting without preferring a suggestion that angels are meant; Wesley makes them all the children of men.

What kind of anointing is meant. Clarke and Barnes read the consecration of kings, priests and prophets by oil, Barnes adding that the oil of gladness suggests a coronation attended with rejoicing; Calvin prefers the anointing of refreshment offered to guests, since the word gladness favours it and Christ is already addressed as on his throne; Robertson allows the same, perhaps the festive anointing on occasions of joy.

How a psalm addressed to Jehovah can be applied to the Son. Barnes argues that an address to Jehovah here would be wholly irrelevant to an argument about angels, and turns the plainness of the psalm's reference to God into a proof of the Son's divinity; Ellicott answers from the psalm's theme, that the Lord shall appear to build up Zion, a hope inseparable from the Messianic promise; Calvin allows that Christ is nowhere named in the psalm and yet holds his kingdom to be avowedly recommended there; Robertson observes only that the word Lord, on which the address turns, is in the Greek version and not in the Hebrew.

Whether the first God in the clause is a second vocative. Barnes says the inserted even weakens the force and that it may be rendered, O God, thy God hath anointed thee, citing Clarke among those who so render it; Clarke allows that translation but is content with the plainer one; Ellicott calls the vocative possible but not probable.
outliers: Clarke alone argues the uniqueness of Christ from the three offices, that some men were kings only, some prophets only, some priests only, and some held two, but none ever held all three in his own person.

Barnes alone rests the application of the psalm on relevance rather than exegesis, asking why a writer arguing that the Son is above angels should suddenly break out in an address to Jehovah, and answering that such is not the manner of Paul or of any other good writer.
Robertson alone notes that the word Lord, on which the whole application of the psalm to the Son depends, stands in the Greek version and not in the Hebrew.

Gill alone draws a cosmological inference from the founding of the earth, that it is the lower part of the creation, that the word denotes stability, and that the clause confutes the notion of an eternal world.
