11.pericope_label: They shall perish; but thou remainest; and they all shall wax old as doth a garment; and as a vesture shalt thou fold them up, and they shall be changed: but thou art the same, and thy years shall not fail. But to which of the angels said he at any time, Sit on my right hand, until I make thine enemies thy footstool?

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin take the manner of the perishing and the session at the right hand. They shall perish means the heavens and the earth, Gill says, not as to the substance of them but as to the quality of them: the present form and fashion of them shall pass away, the curse will be removed from them, and they will be renewed and purified, but the substance of them will continue, otherwise there would be no place either for the righteous or the wicked. On the next verse Gill says that as a vesture shalt thou fold them up means in order to lay them aside and make no use of them in the manner they now are, just as clothes, when they are grown old or out of fashion, are folded up and laid aside from use at present, or are put into another form; in the Hebrew text it is, as a vesture shalt thou change them, but the sense is the same, for a garment is changed by folding it or turning it. On the last verse Gill says that God never said to any of the angels in his council or covenant what is here said: he never designed to give them any such honour as is hereafter expressed, he never promised it to them or bestowed it on them, and he never called up any of them to so high a place or to such a dignity. Calvin says the Apostle again by another testimony extols the excellency of Christ, that it might hence be evident how much he is above the angels, and that the passage cannot be explained of any but of Christ. For as it was not lawful for kings to touch the priesthood, as is testified by the leprosy of Uzziah, and as it appears that neither David nor any other of his successors in the kingdom was ordained a priest, it follows that a new kingdom as well as a new priesthood is here introduced, since the same person is made a king and a priest, Calvin argues; besides, the eternity of the priesthood is suitable to Christ alone. In the beginning of the Psalm he is set at God's right hand, Calvin says, and this form of expression means the same as though it was said that the second place was given him by the Father, for it is a metaphor which signifies that he is the Father's vicegerent and his chief minister in exercising authority, so that the Father rules through him; no one of the angels bears so honourable an office, hence Christ far excels all. As there are never wanting enemies to oppose Christ's kingdom, it seems not to be beyond the reach of danger, Calvin says, especially as they who attempt to overthrow it possess great power, have recourse to various artifices, and make all their attacks with furious violence: doubtless, were we to regard things as they appear, the kingdom of Christ would seem often to be on the verge of ruin. But the promise that Christ shall never be thrust from his seat takes away from us every fear, for he will lay prostrate all his enemies, Calvin says. These two things ought to be borne in mind, that the kingdom of Christ shall never in this world be at rest, but that there will be many enemies by whom it will be disturbed, and secondly, that whatever its enemies may do they shall never prevail, for the session of Christ at God's right hand will not be for a time but to the end of the world, and on this account all who will not submit to his authority shall be laid prostrate and trodden under his feet.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson take the perishing of the heavens, the figure of the vesture and the seventh quotation. They shall perish means they shall pass away or be destroyed, Barnes says, and probably no more is meant by the phrase here than that important changes will take place in them, or that they will change their form; still, it is not possible to foresee what changes may yet take place in the heavenly bodies, or to say that the present universe may not at some period be destroyed and be succeeded by another creation still more magnificent. He that created the universe by a word can destroy it by a word, Barnes says, and he that formed the present frame of nature can cause it to be succeeded by another not less wonderful and glorious, and the Scriptures seem to hold out the idea that the present frame of the universe shall be destroyed. But thou remainest means thou shalt not die or be destroyed, Barnes says: what a sublime thought, that though the heavens and earth should suddenly disappear, or though they should gradually wear out and become extinct, yet there is one infinite Being who remains unaffected and unchanged, and nothing can reach or disturb him. Let us not be alarmed, then, at any revolution, Barnes says: let us not fear, though we should see the heavens rolled up as a scroll and the stars falling from their places, for God, the Creator and Redeemer, presides over all. The word wax is an old Saxon word meaning to grow or increase or become, Barnes notes, and the heavens are here compared with a garment, meaning that as that grows old and decays so it will be with the heavens and the earth: the language is evidently figurative, and yet who can tell how much literal truth there may be couched under it? Is it absurd to suppose that that sun which daily sends forth so many countless millions of beams of light over the universe may, in a course of ages, become diminished in its splendour and shine with feeble lustre? On the next verse Barnes says a vesture is literally something thrown around, denoting properly the outer garment, the cloak or mantle, and that the heavens are represented in the Scriptures as an expanse, and a curtain or tent, and as a scroll that might be spread out or rolled up like a book, while here they are represented as a garment or mantle that might be folded up, the language being borrowed from folding up and laying aside garments that are no longer fit for use. They shall be changed means they shall be exchanged for others, or shall give place to the new heavens and the new earth, Barnes says: the meaning is that the present form of the heavens and the earth is not to be permanent but is to be succeeded by others, while the Creator is to remain the same. What could more clearly prove that he of whom this is spoken is immutable, Barnes asks; yet it is indubitably spoken of the Messiah, and must demonstrate that he is divine, for these attributes cannot be conferred on a creature, and nothing can be clearer than that he who penned the epistle believed that the Son of God was divine. On the last verse Barnes says the apostle adduces one other proof of the exaltation of the Son of God above the angels, asking where there is an instance in which God addressed any one of the angels and asked him to sit at his right hand until he should subdue his enemies under him. Until I make thine enemies thy footstool means until I reduce them to entire subjection, Barnes says: a footstool is what is placed under the feet when we sit on a chair, and the phrase to make an enemy a footstool is borrowed from the custom of ancient warriors, who stood on the necks of vanquished kings on the occasion of celebrating a triumph over them, as a token of their complete prostration. The exaltation of the Redeemer to which the apostle refers here is to the mediatorial throne, Barnes says, in which he is exalted far above the angels: his foes are to be subdued to him, but angels are to be employed as mere instruments in that great work. Ellicott refers the words about waxing old to both the earth and the heavens, citing the prophet that the heavens shall be rolled together as a scroll and that the earth shall wax old like a garment. On the next verse he renders it, and as a mantle shalt thou roll them up, as a garment shall they also be changed, and traces the course of thought: as the garment which has grown old is rolled up and changed, so the former heavens and earth shall give place to the new heavens and the new earth. On the last verse Ellicott says the final appeal is made to that Psalm which more frequently than any other is quoted in reference to Christ, and which is the source of all the New Testament references to the Saviour's session at the right hand of God. That it was regularly understood by the Jews of our Lord's time to be a Messianic Psalm is clear both from the Gospel and from the independent notices which we possess, Ellicott says, and most probably it stands alone amongst the Psalms as being simply prophetic, since its words have never been addressed either to angels or to an earthly king. Robertson notes that shall perish is a future middle, and remarks that modern scientists no longer postulate the eternal existence of the heavenly bodies; but thou continuest is what matters most, the eternal existence of God's Son as Creator and Preserver of the universe. On the next verse Robertson says a mantle is an old word for a covering, used elsewhere in the New Testament of a veil, and that shalt thou roll up is a late form meaning to fold together; they shall be changed is a second future passive of an old verb, and shall not fail is used of the sun elsewhere. Nature is at his mercy, not he at nature's, Robertson quotes. On the last verse he says this seventh quotation is proof of the Son's superiority as the Son of God to angels, and is from a Messianic Psalm frequently quoted in this Epistle; sit thou is an imperative middle, and till I make is an indefinite temporal clause about the future.

Clarke and Wesley take the perishing, the etymology of world and the immutability. They shall perish means that, permanently fixed as they seem to be, a time shall come when they shall be dissolved, and afterward new heavens and a new earth be formed in which righteousness alone shall dwell, Clarke says. Shall wax old as doth a garment means that as a garment by long using becomes unfit to be longer used, so shall all visible things: they shall wear old, and wear out, and hence the necessity of their being renewed. It is remarkable that our word world is a contraction of wear old, Clarke says, a term by which our ancestors expressed the sentiment contained in this verse, and that the word was thus compounded and had this sense in our language may be proved from the most competent witnesses, it having been formerly written weorold and wereld. This etymology is finely alluded to by our excellent poet Spencer, Clarke says, when describing the primitive age of innocence succeeded by the age of depravity, where the lion did with the lamb consort and the dove sat by the falcon's side, but when the World woxe old, it woxe warre old, whereof it hight, and having shortly tried the trains of wit, in wickedness woxe bold. Even the heathen poets are full of such allusions, Clarke adds. Instead of the present tense some good manuscripts read the future, thou shalt remain, Clarke notes, and the difference between these two readings is of little importance. On the next verse Clarke says they shall be changed, not destroyed ultimately or annihilated, but changed and renewed; but thou art the same, and these words can be said of no being but God, since all others are changeable or perishable because temporal, and only that which is eternal can continue essentially the same. Thy years shall not fail, Clarke says: there is in the divine duration no circle to be run, no space to be measured, no time to be reckoned, but all is eternity, infinite and onward. On the last verse Clarke says we have already seen, from the opinions and concessions of the Jews, that if Jesus Christ could be proved to be greater than the angels it would necessarily follow that he was God, and this the apostle does most amply prove by these various quotations from their own Scriptures, for he shows that while he is the supreme and absolute Sovereign they are no more than his messengers and servants, and servants even to his servants, that is, to mankind. Wesley says, as a mantle, means with all ease; they shall be changed into new heavens and a new earth, but thou art eternally the same.

Cyril takes the end of the world and the session. Our Lord Jesus Christ comes from heaven, and he comes with glory at the end of this world, in the last day, Cyril says: for of this world there is to be an end, and this created world is to be re-made anew. For since corruption, and theft, and adultery, and every sort of sins have been poured forth over the earth, and blood has been mingled with blood in the world, therefore, that this wondrous dwelling-place may not remain filled with iniquity, this world passeth away, that the fairer world may be made manifest, Cyril says. And wouldest thou receive the proof of this out of the words of Scripture? Listen to Esaias, saying, And the heaven shall be rolled together as a scroll, and all the stars shall fall as leaves from a vine, and as leaves fall from a fig-tree. On the last verse Cyril returns to the testimonies concerning the Son's sitting at the right hand of the Father, from the Gospel according to Matthew, from Peter, and from the letters to the Romans, the Ephesians and the Colossians, ending with the Epistle to the Hebrews itself.

debates: How completely the heavens perish. Gill says not as to their substance but as to their quality, the form and fashion passing while the substance continues, since otherwise there would be no place for the righteous or the wicked; Clarke says they are changed and renewed, not destroyed ultimately or annihilated; Barnes will not close the question, allowing that the present universe may at some period be destroyed and succeeded by another creation still more magnificent, and asking whether the sun may not in a course of ages shine with feeble lustre; Cyril gives a moral reason rather than a physical one, that the world passes away because it has been filled with iniquity.

Whether the hundred and tenth Psalm is purely prophetic. Ellicott, who has argued that the second Psalm and the forty-fifth both had a first reference to an earthly king, says that most probably this one stands alone among the Psalms as being simply prophetic, its words having never been addressed either to angels or to an earthly king; Calvin reaches the same conclusion by a different route, that since kings might not touch the priesthood and no successor of David was ordained a priest, a new kingdom and a new priesthood are introduced here in one person.

What the immutability proves. Barnes asks what could more clearly prove the speaker immutable, and argues that since the words are indubitably spoken of the Messiah they demonstrate his divinity, such attributes not being conferrable on a creature; Clarke says the words can be said of no being but God, since all others are changeable because temporal; Wesley says only that thou art eternally the same.

What the footstool means. Barnes derives the figure from the custom of ancient warriors who stood on the necks of vanquished kings while celebrating a triumph, and adds that angels are employed as mere instruments in the subduing; Calvin reads the promise as a comfort against appearances, since the kingdom would often seem on the verge of ruin; Clarke draws the chapter's conclusion, that the Son is supreme Sovereign while the angels are servants, and servants even to his servants.
outliers: Clarke alone derives the English word world from wear old, citing the older spellings and quoting a poet on the age when the World woxe old and woxe warre old.

Barnes alone speculates that the sun itself may be exhausting, asking whether it is absurd to suppose that a body sending forth so many countless millions of beams may in a course of ages shine with feeble lustre; Robertson, a century later, records that modern scientists no longer postulate the eternal existence of the heavenly bodies.

Cyril alone explains the end of the world by its moral condition, that since corruption and theft and adultery have been poured forth over the earth and blood mingled with blood, this dwelling-place must pass away that a fairer world may be made manifest.
Clarke alone notes the variant by which some good manuscripts read thou shalt remain for thou remainest, and dismisses the difference as of little importance.

14.pericope_label: Are they not all ministering spirits, sent forth to minister for them who shall be heirs of salvation?

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin take the Jewish phrase and the appointment of the angels. Are they not all ministering spirits means servants to God, to Christ and to his people, and therefore they must be inferior to the Son of God, Gill says. The phrase is Rabbinical: frequent mention is made in Jewish writings of the angels of ministry, or the ministering angels, and this is their common appellation with the Jews, so the apostle, writing to such, uses a like phrase well known to them and appeals to them if the angels were not such spirits. Calvin says that, so the comparison might appear more clearly, he now mentions what the condition of angels is: by calling them spirits he denotes their eminence, for in this respect they are superior to corporal creatures, but the office which he immediately mentions reduces them to their own rank, as it is the reverse of dominion, and this he states still more distinctly when he says that they are sent forth. The first word means that they were officials, Calvin says, but the second imports what is more humble and abject: angels are said to be officially appointed, and they are thus appointed for the purpose of doing service to the heirs of salvation, so that the verse means, are they not all ministrant spirits, sent forth for service, on account of those who are to inherit salvation. They are spirits having a special office allotted them, being sent forth to do service in behalf of those who are heirs of salvation, Calvin says, and it hence appears that they have a special appointment for this purpose. The service which God allots to angels is indeed honourable, Calvin says, but the very fact that they serve shows that they are far inferior to Christ, who is the Lord of all. If any one objects and says that Christ is also called in many places both a servant and a minister, not only to God but also to men, the reply may be readily given, Calvin says: his being a servant was not owing to his nature but to a voluntary humility, and at the same time his sovereignty remained to his nature; but angels, on the other hand, were created for this end, that they might serve, and to minister is what belongs to their condition. The difference then is great, Calvin says, for what is natural to them is as it were adventitious to Christ, because he took our flesh, and what necessarily belongs to them he of his own accord undertook; besides, Christ is a minister in such a way that though he is in our flesh nothing is diminished from the majesty of his dominion. From this passage the faithful receive no small consolation, Calvin says, for they hear that celestial hosts are assigned to them as ministers in order to secure their salvation: it is indeed no common pledge of God's love towards us that they are continually engaged in our behalf, and hence also proceeds a singular confirmation to our faith, that our salvation, being defended by such guardians, is beyond the reach of danger. Well then has God provided for our infirmities by giving us such assistants to oppose Satan, and to put forth their power in every way to defend us, Calvin says; but this benefit he grants especially to his chosen people, hence that angels may minister to us we must be the members of Christ. Yet some testimonies of Scripture may on the other hand be adduced to show that angels are sometimes sent forth for the sake of the reprobate, Calvin notes, for mention is made by Daniel of the angels of the Persians and the Greeks; but to this I answer that they were in such a way assisted by angels that the Lord might thus promote the salvation of his own people, for their success and their victories had always a reference to the benefit of the Church. This is certain, Calvin concludes, that as we have been banished by sin from God's kingdom we can have no communion with angels except through the reconciliation made by Christ, and this we may see by the ladder shown in a vision to the patriarch Jacob.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson take the word for ministering, the direction of the service and the question of guardian angels. There is not one of the angels that is elevated to the high rank of the Redeemer, Barnes says: even the most exalted angel is employed in the comparatively humble office of a ministering spirit appointed to aid the heirs of salvation. A ministering spirit is one employed to execute the will of God, and the proper meaning of the word here, whence our word liturgy comes, is pertaining to public service, or the service of the people, applied particularly to those who were engaged in the public service of the temple, Barnes says: they were those who rendered aid to others, who were helpers or servants, and such is the meaning here, since they are employed to render aid or assistance to Christians. Sent forth means appointed by God for this, Barnes says: they are sent, are under his control, are in a subordinate capacity, as Gabriel was sent forth to convey an important message to Daniel. They are called heirs of salvation because they are adopted into the family of God and are treated as his sons, Barnes says, and the main point here is that the angels are employed in a much more humble capacity than the Son of God, and therefore that he sustains a far more elevated rank. But while the apostle has proved this, he has incidentally stated an exceedingly interesting doctrine, that the angels are employed to further the salvation of the people of God, Barnes says, and in this doctrine there is nothing absurd: it is no more improbable that angels should be employed to aid man than that one man should aid another, certainly not as improbable as that the Son of God should come down not to be ministered unto but to minister. Indeed, it is a great principle of the divine administration that one class of God's creatures are to minister to others, Barnes says, that one is to aid another, to assist him in trouble, to provide for him when poor, and to counsel him in perplexity: God has appointed parents to aid their children, neighbours to aid their neighbours, the rich to aid the poor, and all over the world the principle is seen that one is to derive benefit from the aid of others. Why may not the angels be employed in this service, Barnes asks: they are pure, benevolent, powerful, and as man was ruined in the fall by the temptation offered by one of an angelic though fallen nature, why should not others of angelic, unfallen holiness come to assist in repairing the evils which their fallen, guilty brethren have inflicted on the race? To me there seems to be a beautiful propriety in bringing aid from another race, as ruin came from another race, Barnes says, and that as those endowed with angelic might, though with fiendish malignity, ruined man, those with angelic might but heavenly benevolence should aid in his recovery and salvation. Farther, it is from the necessity of the case a great principle that the weak shall be aided by the strong, the ignorant by the enlightened, the impure by the pure, the tempted by those who have not fallen by temptation, Barnes adds, and all over the world we see this in operation, so why shall it not be extended to the inhabitants of other abodes? Ellicott says that in this verse and the preceding is repeated the contrast of the earlier verses in reversed order, the words ministering spirits at once recalling the ministers and winds spoken of before, since the same Greek word stands for winds and spirits. In the Greek version this word minister is usually applied to those who stood before God in his earthly sanctuary, Ellicott says, so here it is fitly used of the nobler offices of the unseen world. To the English reader it may seem that those who in the earlier verse are God's ministers are here represented as servants of man, Ellicott says, but it is not really so, for the words properly mean sent forth, that is, continually sent forth, to do service to God, for the sake of them who are to inherit salvation. Inherit is a prelude of what follows in the next chapter, Ellicott adds, and the last word, salvation, expresses the divine purpose indicated by all the prophecies that have passed under review: the chapter has been occupied with promises of the Christ, and the last word brings before us Jesus, the Saviour. Robertson says the adjective for ministering was not found in profane authors, according to the lexicon, but occurs in the papyri for a work tax, money in place of service, and for religious service also. Sent forth is a present passive participle, sent forth repeatedly, from time to time as occasion requires, Robertson says, and the preposition has its usual causal meaning; that shall inherit means that are going to inherit, destined to inherit, and salvation is here used of the final salvation in its consummation. We do not have here the doctrine of special guardian angels for each of us, Robertson says, but simply the fact that angels are used for our good; and he quotes a contemporary writer asking whether, if so, we may not be aided, inspired and guided by a cloud of witnesses, not witnesses only but helpers, agents like ourselves of the immanent God.

Clarke and Wesley take the force of the question and the condition of the inheritance. Are they not all ministering spirits means that they are all ministering spirits, Clarke says, for the Hebrews often express the strongest affirmative by an interrogation: all the angels, even those of the highest order, are employed by their Creator to serve those who believe in Christ Jesus. What these services are, and how performed, it would be impossible to state, Clarke says: much has been written on the subject, partly founded on Scripture and partly on conjecture, and they are no doubt constantly employed in averting evil and procuring good. If God help man by man, we need not wonder that he helps man by angels, Clarke says: we know that he needs none of those helps, for he can do all things himself, yet it seems agreeable to his infinite wisdom and goodness to use them; this is part of the economy of God in the government of the world and of the Church, and a part, no doubt, essential to the harmony and perfection of the whole. Clarke refers the reader to a sermon on this text in the works of John Wesley, and to a large treatment of the subject by another commentator, which he calls a very learned, judicious and important work, but by far too diffuse, in which the words of God are drowned in the sayings of man. The Godhead of Christ is a subject of such great importance, both to the faith and hope of a Christian, that I feel it necessary to bring it full into view wherever it is referred to in the sacred writings, Clarke adds: it is a prominent article in the apostle's creed, and should be so in ours. Wesley says, Are they not all, though of various orders, ministering spirits, sent forth, ministering before God, sent forth to men, to attend on them in numerous offices of protection, care and kindness, who, having patiently continued in welldoing, shall inherit everlasting salvation.

debates: Whom the angels serve. Barnes says they render aid to Christians; Ellicott denies that those who are God's ministers a few verses earlier are here made servants of man, and renders the words, sent forth to do service to God, for the sake of them who are to inherit salvation; Calvin separates the two Greek words, an official appointment and the work to be done, and renders it, sent forth for service, on account of those who are to inherit salvation; Wesley divides the phrase between the two, ministering before God and sent forth to men.

Whether the verse teaches guardian angels. Robertson denies that we have here the doctrine of special guardian angels for each of us, allowing only that angels are used for our good; Calvin speaks of celestial hosts assigned to us as ministers and of our salvation being defended by such guardians, but restricts the benefit to the chosen, since to be ministered to by angels we must be members of Christ; Wesley speaks of numerous offices of protection, care and kindness without raising the question.

Why it is fitting that angels should help men at all. Barnes argues from the general principle that one class of creatures ministers to another, parents to children and the rich to the poor, and adds a symmetry, that since ruin came to man from another race it is fitting that aid should come from the same race; Clarke says only that if God helps man by man we need not wonder that he helps man by angels, though he needs no such helps; Calvin makes it a pledge of God's love that they are continually engaged in our behalf.

Who the heirs are. Barnes says they are called heirs because adopted into the family of God and treated as his sons; Calvin restricts the ministry of angels to the chosen people and answers the objection from the angels of the Persians and the Greeks by saying their victories always had reference to the benefit of the Church; Wesley alone attaches a condition, that those who inherit are those who have patiently continued in welldoing.
outliers: Barnes alone finds a symmetry in the arrangement, that as those endowed with angelic might but fiendish malignity ruined man, those with angelic might and heavenly benevolence should repair the ruin, so that aid comes from the race that brought the harm.

Clarke alone names a living contemporary in his notes, recommending a sermon of John Wesley's on this text, and in the same breath dismisses a rival commentator's treatment as learned and judicious but by far too diffuse, the words of God being drowned in the sayings of man.
Robertson alone quotes a physicist of his own day on the question, asking whether we may not be aided and guided by helpers who are agents, like ourselves, of the immanent God.
Wesley alone makes the inheritance conditional, adding that those who inherit everlasting salvation are those who have patiently continued in welldoing.
